#1049. Odegaard winner spares officials from bizarre VAR row

An ultimately routine Arsenal win but, even by the standards of VAR, an utterly bizarre refereeing controversy. Mikel Arteta’s instant simmering fury at being denied a first-half penalty may also have turned into something rather more explosive had Martin Odegaard not later sent the champions six points clear with a ninth win in 10 Premier League games.

The big talking point arose with inadvertent theatre from referee Farai Hallam when Kai Havertz, who was clearly in an offside position, was equally clearly pulled down by Hull City defender Nobel Mendy inside the penalty area. Which came first? The intervention of VAR suggested the latter. But Hallam duly went to check the pitch-side monitor before then announcing the former.

“After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No 32 on Red No 29,” the referee declared. Cue cheers from the home Arsenal crowd. “However…,” he went on. “Red No 29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City.”

#ARSHUL – 42' VAR recommended an on-field review for a potential penalty to Arsenal for a challenge by Mendy on Havertz - but determined that Havertz was in an offside position in the build-up. REF: "After review, there is a holding offence by Blue No.32 on Red No.29. However, Red No.29 is in an offside position, so the final decision will be a free-kick for offside to Hull City".

It all sounded so decisive that most inside the Emirates instinctively thought the outcome reasonable. But then came a closer look at the rules. And Law 11.2 certainly did seem to support Arteta’s protestations: “In situations where a player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

Arteta clearly saw no value after the match in aiming much criticism at Hallam following a fourth 1-0 win in 10 league games, but did still emphasise his surprise at the decision. “What do you think?” he asked one reporter. “I thought offside, but the law says that doesn’t matter,” replied the journalist. “So not offside then,” said Arteta, who stressed that he needs to understand “what is overruling what in the decision-making” after a Premier League statement simply said that Havertz was deemed offside “in the build-up”.

At the very best, it all leaves further confusion and again opens refereeing body Pro Ref to the charge of inconsistency. Fabian Schär, for example, was awarded a penalty for Newcastle against Bournemouth in 2024, despite being in an offside position when his shirt was grabbed by Adam Smith.

Conversely, Dango Ouattara had a penalty overturned for Brentford against Leeds last season after going down under pressure from Gabriel Gudmundsson before being deemed offside. The crucial point seems to be whether the player has actually challenged for the ball at the time of the infringement and, in this case, the answer was surely “no”.

Premier League title triumphs, however, are often forged on forgettable wins in frustrating circumstances and this was ultimately a classic of the genre. With Noni Madueke continuing to step up superbly in the absence of Bukayo Saka, Arsenal’s combination of attacking persistence and defensive resilience was ultimately rewarded by Odegaard’s scrappy 72nd-minute shot. For young players, it was also every bit as educational as the VAR controversy might be for emerging officials.

Madueke’s low shot forced a save by Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, but Odegaard was somehow first to the rebound, despite being the wrong side of the penalty spot and five yards behind Hull defender John Egan when the ball was struck.

“The way he scores, not the most beautiful, but the most effective,” said Arteta, who said that his team had sometimes tried too hard for a “perfect goal” and should instead be happy with something “more pragmatic”.

It was a well-judged assessment as Arsenal head into the international break with creative deficiencies, but still almost flawless in the cold hard currency of results. Three wins in three days, including at Anfield and in Prague, also underlines a certain champions mentality.

“I need to praise the players,” said Arteta. “It’s been very very demanding; very short time to recover with all the travel. The mentality is incredible. It’s still going to be super difficult. We can improve in a number of areas.”

When it was then put to him that Arsenal have been offside 35 times this season – with Havertz responsible for 15 of those – Arteta acknowledged that “timing” was one element. But, with Havertz targeted by some frustrated fans, he stressed that responsibility was always shared for those split-second moments by the passer and receiver.

He also singled out Madueke, again easily Arsenal’s most creative player, following his surprise omission from Thomas Tuchel’s England squad. “He went away, started to train, he came back and it was a different Noni,” said Arteta, of his reaction to also being out of the Arsenal team earlier in the season. “You could sense that he meant business and he wasn’t going to accept the situation and, since then, I think he’s been incredible.”

An improved showing by Jaissle’s Newcastle, but they will be dissapointed that they failed to see it through after Jacob Murphy scored in the 80th minute.

Arsenal far from their best, but it is another one-goal win in the Premier League. They are now six points clear at the top of the Premier League, and it is 27 points from the first 30 available.

Another save at Craven Cottage, this time from Hornicek to keep out a sweet strike from Sessegnon at the edge of the box. Moments earlier, Dedic brought down Muniz at the edge of the box.

One last change by Arteta: Zubmimendi on for Guimaraes. Madueke could have made the points safe after slick interplay involving Eze and Merino around the edge of the box. Tried to be clever with the finish, the goalkeeper’s save was deflected back towards the goal and it was hacked off the line.

Leno gets down quickly to deny Lewis Hall as Newcastle pour forward in search of the winner.

As good as Murphy’s goal was, Rodrigo Muniz’s finish with the outside of his foot may well be better. Newcastle’s lead was short-lived.

And they have immediately conceded an equaliser, Rodrigo Munoz with a smart close range finish but Newcastle were be mortified with the defending.

Not for the first time Will Osula’s weak hold up play gives the ball back to Fulham but Newcastle had plenty of men back and failed to clear.

Jacob Murphy has scored the goal that some of Newcastle’s earlier good play deserved. Cut inside on to his weaker left foot, and curled a shot beyond Leno from 20 yards.

Newcastle finally have their goal and what a strike it is from Jacob Murphy. A loose pass from Cesar Palacios in midfield gifted possession to the Newcastle winger and he ran forward, cut inside on to his left foot and curled a shot beyond the reach of Leno from 25 yards.

Arsenal’s captain dinks over Tzolakis after Hull’s goalkeeper saved Madueke’s shot. Odeegard was on the move while the defenders were on their heels. Relief at the Emirates, this has been hard work for the champions. Can Hull muster a response?

Arteta with a double sub: Gyokeres and Merino on for Havertz and Rice, which comes as something of a surprise.

Hull’s goalkeeper Tzolakis has just saved with his feet to deny Madueke. A few minutes earlier, Konsa blocked a Cho shot after a threatening Hull break. Still no opening goal.

The second halves at the Emirates and Craven Cottage have kicked off. No changes from Arsenal, Hull, Fulham or Newcastle.

The law states: “A player in an offside position is moving towards the ball with the intention of playing the ball and is fouled before playing or attempting to play the ball, or challenging an opponent for the ball, the foul is penalised as it has occurred before the offside offence.”

Hopefully there will be more action in the second 45 minutes at Craven Cottage and the Emirates.

An odd moment at the Emirates. Referee Farai Hallam was sent to monitor to look at a shirt pull on Kai Havertz in the Hull box. Through his headset, he tells the crowd that a “holding offence” has been committed – cue cheers from the Arsenal fans – before adding “however, the Arsenal player was in an offside position”. So no penalty. It would have been very soft in any case, Havertz was not close to reaching the rebound from a long shot.

Mikel Arteta predictably furious to not get a penalty, even though Havertz was clearly offside before being pulled.

David Raya to Arsenal’s rescue, plucking Stroud’s shot away from the bottom corner after a Calafiori giveaway. This has been a positive opening 20 minutes from Hull.

Arsenal with a penalty shout, turned down.

Kai Havertz was going away from goal but Nobel Medy hardly subtle with his challenge – arm and leg – on the edge of the area. It would have been what we call soft but the sort of innocuous challenge that very often results in a foul elsewhere on the pitch.

On a self-indulgent note, this is an all-too-rare trip to the Emirates for me. I covered Arsenal for the last decade of the Arsene Wenger era, ending in 2018 and haven’t made many visits since. A few things are already striking: so many familiar faces still among the staff at a club that has always had more of a family feel than most. Outside, and few of the gaps in the middle (or top tier) that became evident during the final Wenger years when many fans clearly lost faith in the team’s title-winning credentials. The atmosphere is a notch up too.

Thiaw heads wide after a well-worked short corner from Newcastle, but the flag is up for offside in any case. Lewis Hall with the cross.

A decent start from Newcastle United against Fulham and you can see clearer patterns of play emerging. The fact that Fulham are constantly looking to build their attacks by playing out from the back has also helped. The home side have had a couple of scares already.

Hull gain some territory in the early exchanges, and win a corner via a long throw. From the set-piece, Egan’s set-piece hit the side-netting. A shot across Arsenal’s bows.

The lack of Mohamed Beloloumi’s creative spark clearly a big blow for Hull against the best defence in the league; a defence that will be further strengthened by the imminent return of William Saliba. Mikel Arteta had decided that Saliba would be better served by playing against Aston Villa for the Under-21s at Boreham Wood tomorrow. Hull have started on the front, though, in the opening minutes

Updates to follow from the Emirates and Craven Cottage. The Last Post was played and there was a minute’s silence as both grounds mark Remembrance Day.

It’s always great to be back home. It’s the last game before the international break so we know the importance of that and the challenges Hull will provide today. We’re super focused, it’s a massive game for us.

With the amount of games we’re playing, we need that freshness. The team has been performing really well, the finishers have been key again and that’s what we have today – start the game really, really strong and if we need to, have the ability to change the game.

Arsenal’s manager says the centre-back will play an Under-21s game tomorrow as the continues his recovery from a back injury.

Arteta says: “In regards to Willy as well, he needs some minutes. Obviously, the Champions League allows you to bring more players into the bench, but we believe that it’s the best thing to do: to play some minutes at the weekend with the Under-21s and then be fully fit for the international break.”

Arsenal are playing very good football, no matter Champions League or Premier League. They are very strong, they control everything not just against us, also other better clubs. But in football, we have a chance. Obviously, they are a big favourite, and we can start to try to create some difficulties for them.

The return of Sean Steur is a positive move from Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle but is it also a sign the German is feeling the pressure of public opinion on Tyneside?

The 18-year-old has looked the best of Newcastle’s summer signings but Newcastle are understandably trying to ease the teenager into things.

Ultimately, though, Steur is the only midfield player who can take possession of the ball under pressure and despite his tender years they have looked a better side with him in it.

There have been widespread calls for Steur to be called back into the side and Jaissle has done just that for a game he could really do with winning coming off the back of four defeats in their last five games.

Malick Thiaw also comes back into the side for Fabian Schar, with Jacob Murphy preferred to Anthony Elanga and Yoane Wissa starting in place of Joe Willock. I don’t think any of those dropped can have any complaints.

However, the constant chopping and changing betrays the problems Jaissle is facing. Whatever team he sends out is struggling to deliver what he wants, both individually and collectively.

With the international break coming up, Newcastle need a positive result to quieten the negative noise.

A big blow for Hull to be without their most inventive and dangerous attacking player. It looks like Sergej Jakirovic has switched things up with a 5-3-2, and it will be a back five not a three for long periods.

No William Saliba in the squad despite his inclusion in the Champions League, although you are allowed more subs on the bench in that competition. Otherwise, Arsenal as expected with Arteta deciding against picking a team without Rice.

🔴 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 ⚪️ Let's get it, Gunners 👊 🤝 @deel

Mikel Arteta has said Arsenal are “looking after” Declan Rice more now than in any previous campaign and has rejected suggestions that the England midfielder is being overplayed.

Rice played through nerve pain in his hamstring in the second half of last season, when he made an extraordinary 69 appearances for club and country.

The 27-year-old has played at least 60 matches in each of the past four campaigns, prompting concerns among Arsenal supporters that he is at risk of burnout or injury.

Arteta kept Rice on the field for the full 90 minutes of Arsenal’s midweek victory over Slavia Prague but insisted the club is working harder than ever to manage the midfielder’s workload.

So far this season, Rice has been left out of Arsenal’s two Carabao Cup matches and also withdrew from the previous international break in September.

Asked if he was concerned about Rice’s fitness, Arteta said: “Concerns? Which is the only player, the only player in this squad, that for two games in the Carabao Cup has been left out of the squad? At home with two days off? It’s not true [that Rice is being overplayed].

“We are really looking after him more than any other season. The way he is training and all the love [he is being shown]. That’s it.

“Here are the demands of this football club and a player like him. Not only him, because there are many others that have even less time. That’s it. That has to be the mindset. If you start to put other things in your brain, [it will create] damage. Erase them, get them in the bin and just focus on what you have to do.”

Newly-promoted Hull City stunned Arsenal at the Emirates thanks to goals from Geovanni and Daniel Cousin in September 2008, but you will find long odds on them repeating the feat this afternoon.

With Manchester City playing at Nottingham Forest in the later kick-off, Mikel Arteta’s team have the chance to extend their lead at the top of the Premier League and make it 27 points from a possible 30 going into the international break.

Victory at Anfield last weekend was achieved with steel and resolve, but the more intricate side of Arsenal’s attacking play will be under the microscope against opponents likely to defend deep and in numbers.

With that in mind, it was noteworthy that Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Bruno Guimaraes and Myles Lewis-Skelly started the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on the bench, with only Odegaard coming on.

Declan Rice played the full 90 minutes, and one wonders if this is a rare chance for Arteta to leave him out of a Premier League starting XI.

Hull are 12th and have lost only two league games, a performance which far exceeds the gloomy pre-season forecasts for their chances. However, they are winless since the end of August and have not kept a clean sheet since a goalless draw with Aston Villa on Sept 4.

There is one other three o’clock kick-off: Fulham host Newcastle United at Craven Cottage, with Matthias Jaissle under increasing pressure.

Newcastle were booed off at St James’ Park on Monday after their limp defeat by Everton, and have looked far too easy to play through all season, with their defensive statistics making for grim reading.

Alvaro Arbeloa was in Jaissle’s position a few weeks ago, but Fulham appear to have turned a corner and were impressive in a 1-1 at Villa Park last time out. There were reports of dressing room unrest, but Fulham rank highly for possession and chance creation so it appears the Spaniard is putting his stamp on things.

#1045. Quantum-enhanced sensing with 500 photons via Fock-space confocal focusing

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Quantum metrology promises measurement precision beyond classical limits by exploiting large-scale quantum states1,2,3,4,5,6,7, yet realizing this advantage faces two fundamental challenges: the deterministic preparation of non-trivial quantum probes8,9 and the efficient extraction of metrological information in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces10,11,12. Here, we introduce quantum confocal microscopy in Fock space that addresses these challenges for a Fock-like probe state with a tightly concentrated photon-number distribution. Drawing a direct analogy between classical wave optics and quantum state evolution in a bosonic mode13,14, we construct a confocal lens system with a quantum circuit of \({\mathcal{O}}(1)\) operational depth, realizing a bidirectional transformation between a readily obtainable coherent state and this Fock-like probe state. Using a superconducting circuit quantum electrodynamics platform, we deterministically prepare focused probe states with mean photon numbers up to N = 500, achieving a 21.5 ± 1.1 dB reduction of the photon-number variance relative to a coherent state. Using the focused states for displacement sensing, we achieve a record metrological gain of 19.20 ± 0.20 dB beyond the standard quantum limit. This work establishes quantum confocal microscopy as a compact protocol that makes high-photon-number non-Gaussian Fock-like probes experimentally accessible and measurable, providing a viable route towards quantum-enhanced precision measurement, and is readily extendable to other bosonic platforms and high-dimensional quantum many-body systems.

#1043. From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.

But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.

Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.

The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

Eight games without a clean sheet underlines their vulnerability and Maresca has much to ponder over the international break with his team six points behind leaders Arsenal.

What a response from Nottingham Forest to Oliver Glasner’s brutal “no-compromises” rant last weekend, as the home team secured only the second league win in front of their own supporters this year.

It was a former City player, Liam Delap, who tormented them with two brilliant individual goals to give Glasner what he hopes will finally be lift-off.

"The day that Delap ARRIVES" 🤩 Nottingham Forest regain their two-goal lead! https://t.co/5yk5eIhPhe

Forest’s £50m record signing was on the 55-man list for Thomas Tuchel’s latest England squad and more performances like this will enhance his chances of senior recognition. It was the archetypal “No 9” performance.

While Forest will hope this proves a turning point in their season, these are certainly worrying times for City.

Marc Guéhi and Josko Gvardiol are both badly out of form and were replaced at half-time with injuries, while it was another alarming evening for goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Despite a brief rally early in the second half, City never looked capable of ending their slump. Even the sight of Manchester United in the bottom three will have done little to cheer their supporters.

Maresca said: “I’m always concerned, even when we win games. We won seven in a row and we have now lost three, so over the break we need to understand what we can do better.

Forest’s home results have been poor for some time, but this was their best performance under Glasner, with the club’s owner Evangelos Marinakis making his first appearance of the season.

“There are a lot of things to improve, he’s still a young man in only his second regular Premier League season. The strike with his left foot is something you either have or you don’t have.”

Forest had started brightly and it was their Brazilian international, Jair Cunha, who finally ended their wait of 8½ hours for a home goal.

It was another City mistake, with Gvardiol dispossessed by Cunha after a poor touch, with the defender advancing into the area to slot his shot into the corner.

#1039. Could AI give NFTs a second chance?

NFTs have plunged in value since their pandemic height in 2021. In some cases, they are worth 99% less than they were paid for. Yet tokenization of real-world assets and AI means the curios may yet have a future.

Remember the NFT boom of 2021? The surge in trading of non-fungible tokens (NFTs), which are unique, blockchain-recorded digital assets, was one of the stranger economic offshoots of the COVID-19 pandemic.

What started as a marginal curiosity became a highly lucrative sector worth close to $40 billion (€36 billion) globally by the end of 2021, almost as valuable as the global art market itself.

In the highly publicized bust that followed, many NFTs lost practically all their value. The wider cryptocurrency crash was particularly punishing for digital collectibles and largely, they have not recovered.

The sector is worth up to 97% less than it was at its height in January 2022, and sales continue to plummet. So far this year, total global sales of NFTs are less than $2 billion, according to FindWeb3, a cryptocurrency and blockchain jobs platform. That's more than 90% down from the peaks of 2021 and 2022.

Does that mean that NFTs will ultimately fade away to nothing, proving right those who dismissed them as a worthless fad? Or is there still some kind of future for them?

"NFTs will still exist, but it will be a niche collectible market," Ben Charoenwong, associate professor of finance at the business school INSEAD, said. "This doesn't mean there cannot be booms here and there, but certainly not take off as people had imagined in the past."

He thinks whatever future it can have will be "narrow" and says doubt is growing over the value of "non-fungible" as a concept. Non-fungible means an asset is unique and cannot be traded like for like, whereas fungible means it can be traded like for like, for example, with money.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He notes that the recent trend of financial institutions converting real-world financial assets, such as bonds and stocks, into digital tokens recorded on a blockchain — the so-called tokenization boom — mostly relates to fungible assets.

However, Andrea Barbon, a finance professor at the University of St Gallen in Switzerland, thinks part of NFTs' future lies in this tokenization boom, as there are some examples of people trading unique real-world assets as NFTs.

"NFT technology is really about ownership," he says. "They describe the ownership of a specific asset that could be a digital asset or real-world asset." He says things like real-estate contracts, expensive watches, artworks or luxury sports cars can now be tokenized, with NFTs created to represent these physical objects.

That immediately begs the question: Why would anyone want to have a digital, NFT version of their watch or sports car?

"Some people want to just speculate on the value of the physical asset and for them, it's great that you don't need to move the physical object around," Barbon said.

"If the object is a nice painting and you buy it from the US, you want to ship it to the UK, that's very costly, it's hassle and it's potentially not safe if the value of this painting is very high," he explained.

He says some companies, such as Courtyard.io, keep physical vaults to hold physical assets which are traded online as NFTs. He says very often, the owner has no interest in having physical possession of the asset.

Another area where he sees some promise for the future of NFTs is connected to artificial intelligence. He says NFTs could help with AI safety, as they could be used to provide unique, verifiable, non-fungible identities for AI agents.

Ethereum and other blockchain providers are in the process of trying to build NFT systems that would represent and verify AI agents, something Barbon says could be very successful.

He envisages a scenario where AI agents are recorded on an NFT blockchain and can then be identified and rated for safety and reliability.

"Everybody else can then see that the AI agent is actually doing well, you can trust it, it's safe," he says. "In order to do that, you need something which is uniquely attached to each AI agent and that can be an NFT."

Another possible use he sees for NFTs in the AI era is that writers and artists could tokenize their work as NFTs so that if an AI agent ends up using it for training, the original work can be more easily identified as unique to the creator.

"Maybe you could then claim that the AI company has to pay you because they have used your content," Barbon says.

While the NFT craze of 2021 can now be seen as a classic bubble, many of those who invested in it have moved on to memecoins and other forms of fungible cryptocurrency, according to Ben Charoenwong.

"Overall, I think the market did not reject blockchains; it rejected non-fungibility," he says.

At the time of the craze, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said NFT popularity was "100% based on the greater fool theory," the idea being that one can make money through the purchase of overvalued, fundamentally worthless assets as long as there is a"greater fool" willing to pay even more.

One of the most famous NFT collections was the Bored Ape Yacht Club, a series of drawings of apes in various locations in various states of boredom. "Obviously, expensive digital images of monkeys are going to improve the world immensely," Gates joked.

In many ways, that collection's current status epitomizes NFTs' fall from grace better than anything else. Although it remains one of the biggest NFT marketplaces, its value has plunged.

The singer Justin Bieber bought one image for 500 ETH (Ethereum), or around $1.3 million dollars. The value fell by around 99% to around $14,000.  He still owns it.

Yet the fact that these images still command such prices shows they are not entirely worthless. That offers some hope to those who still believe in the technology. Alongside other possible applications linked to AI and tokenization, NFTs may still have a future, albeit a more modest one than when they first came to public attention.

#1037. Liverpool fans are enjoying watching their team again as they close in on Champions League qualification after Club Brugge victory... now it's time for Andoni Iraola to make it a perfect week at Everton, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 17:09 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 18:48 EST, 25 November 2026

Andoni Iraola tried to stifle a smirk on Tuesday when it was put to him that he had a fair chance of completing a perfect week by thrashing Manchester United, winning away in Europe and then winning his first-ever Merseyside Derby.

The usual responses came back of remaining level-headed and not getting carried away, of course – but Iraola has ticked off two of those three tasks and now goes to Everton with his much-criticised, big-money signings in the form of their Liverpool careers.

That is Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz, of course, who both scored here to further quash any narratives over them being expensive flops, a debate which had followed them for much of their first year or so on Merseyside.

Isak scored a brace to take his season tally to double-figures and make it six away games in a row where he has struck, while Wirtz followed up his best performance of the season against United with a fine strike from distance.

Wirtz especially has never been far away from criticism during his time at the club but is silencing his doubters every week and said this week that Iraola had helped him rediscover the player Liverpool thought they were buying for £116million two summers ago.

The sentiment spreads beyond Wirtz. After a season of strife, Iraola has brought the feel-good factor back at Anfield and supporters are enjoying watching their team again after a year in which it felt like a chore to do so some weeks.

Alexander Isak scored twice as Liverpool beat Club Brugge 3-0 in the Champions League

That made it three wins in a row for the Reds as they start to really click under Andoni Iraola

CLUB BRUGGE (4-3-3): Sommer 4; Sabbe 5 (Siquet 84), Spileers 5, Mechele 6, Seys 6; Vetlesen 6 (Vermant 75), Potts 7 (Tsawa 84), Vanaken 6; Forbs 7, Tresoldi 6, Lemarechal 7 (Diakhon 75).

Subs not used: Jackers, Vanden Driessche, Han-beom Lee, Virgili, Dams, Robberechts, Audoor, Vasovic.

LIVERPOOL (4-2-3-1): Alisson 7; Frimpong 6 (Van Dijk 73, 6), Araujo 6, Jacquet 7, Kerkez 6; Nyoni 7 (Mac Allister 73, 6), Szoboszlai 7; Munoz 6 (Ngumoha 42, 6), Wirtz 7, Barcola 6 (Chambers 86); ISAK 8 (Koumas 86).

Subs not used: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Tsimikas, McConnell, Danns.

It is making the Liverpool fans fall for Iraola a little bit more each week. How that feeling would be turbocharged with Derby delight at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Sunday.

‘I was very pleased with the result and the performance overall,’ said Iraola. ‘At 3-0, you can think it was an easy game and I don’t think it was. We were facing a really good team.’

As the 1,000 or so travelling Kop enjoyed their strong Belgian beers and chocolate waffles in this quaint, picturesque city, they were still laughing about poor old Manchester United and Sunday’s 4-0 demolition job.

This was a much tougher test against an opposition that had started well in the Champions League with three wins from four, so Liverpool’s performance was never going to be as convincing – but the victory was still important.

It helped them take a step closer to cementing a top eight place in this long-winded league phase. That would ease the pressure on a congested calendar by seeing them not only be able to rest players in the latter games of the league stage but also skip a play-off round.

Club Brugge are no mugs and they showed that, with energetic winger Carlos Forbs the pick of the bunch. The former Manchester City academy starlet has inherited a certain Cristiano Ronaldo’s No 7 shirt at Portugal and gave Milos Kerkez a testing night here.

The Belgian side, like Liverpool, had won three of their first four European games including victory away to Inter. They had won five of the last seven league titles with a brave playing style that Iraola admitted was a pleasure to analyse – which he added was not always the case.

Their bold approach was their undoing here, though, with possession tossed away far too easily for Liverpool’s opener after 13 minutes. Yann Sommer, in the winter of his career at 37, passed straight to Bradley Barcola who, via stand-in skipper Dominik Szoboszlai, found Isak.

The Swede needed no second invitation to fire home his ninth goal of the season. Isak had been rested for most of Liverpool’s early European outings but was the difference here and loves playing away: he has now netted on his last six games away from Anfield.

Liverpool have 12 points from five games and will almost certainly be in the knockout stages

Florian Wirtz continued his fine form as he curled in a delightful effort to put Liverpool 2-0 up

Iraola will hope to make it the perfect week with victory in Sunday's Merseyside Derby

Only Mohamed Salah has done so in seven or more in recent history for Liverpool. Everton would be a fine place to match that record.

Despite the scoreline flattering Liverpool, things were far from easy after Isak’s opener. Alisson was needed to deny Felix Lemarechal both sides at half-time and Virgil van Dijk – rested from the start – was called on as a second-half substitute to steady the ship.

Winger Victor Munoz limped off in agony after going down before half-time holding his knee. Iraola feared the worst when a stretcher was called but the Spaniard walked off and was feeling ‘optimistic’ after the match, according to the boss.

Szoboszlai should have put the game to bed after a sublime team move led to the Hungarian being thwarted by Sommer at point-blank range, while Barcola was also guilty of wastefulness after getting his feet tangled up when in a dangerous position.

But Wirtz, in the best form of his Liverpool career, made it three goals in his last three with a fine strike from distance that clipped in off the post.

Then Isak raced through on goal and dinked a shot over Sommer for goal No 10 of the season for him. It completed a memorable night for Iraola and his big-money boys. Now to make it a perfect week at Everton on Sunday.

#1033. A gut–brain sensory-motor circuit regulates sugar ingestion in Drosophila

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Bidirectional communication between the brain and digestive tract is critical for optimizing nutrient preference and food intake, yet the neural mechanisms that couple gut nutrient sensing with ingestive motor control remain poorly understood. Here we identify a gut–brain sensory-motor circuit that regulates sugar ingestion in flies. We show that the brain neurons that regulate food ingestion, IN1s1, receive excitatory input from enteric sensory neurons that penetrate the foregut epithelium and detect sugars in the gut lumen during ingestion. Functional imaging and connectome analyses reveal that IN1s integrate excitatory input from multiple sugar-sensing neurons, including enteric sensory neurons, and provide inhibitory output to enteric motor neurons that control the muscles at the entry of the crop—a stomach-like organ. During ingestion, IN1 activation suppresses these enteric motor neurons, relaxes the crop duct and promotes rapid transfer of food into the crop, thereby enabling sustained food intake. Together, our findings describe a gut–brain circuit that controls the motor activity of digestive tract muscles during feeding and suggest a circuit mechanism by which nutrient signals from the gut contribute to the dynamic regulation of food intake across metabolic states.

a, Schematic of the two-photon microscope setup coupled with optogenetic stimulation. A male fly is standing on top of an air-suspended spherical treadmill (PMT, photomultiplier tube, LED, light-emitting diode). b, Schematic showing the strategy used for optogenetic stimulation coupled with two-photon calcium imaging. GCaMP6s is expressed in IN1s, while the red-shifted opsin, Chrimson, is expressed in sensory neurons. c-m, Normalized (ΔF/F0) GCaMP6s fluorescence in IN1s before and after optogenetic stimulation of candidate sensory neurons: Control group (c), sugar sensing neurons: Gr5a (d), Gr43a (e), Gr64a (f), Gr64c (g), Gr64d (h), Gr64e (i), Gr64f (j), bitter sensing neurons, Gr66a (k), water sensing neurons, ppk28 (l), and mechanosensory neurons, TMC (m). The optogenetic stimulation period is indicated in a magenta-shaded area (n = 5-8 males per genotype, 3-5 trials per fly, mean ± s.e.m., stimulation duration = 1s, continuous, power = ~0.75 mW). n, Normalized peak responses of IN1s in indicated genotypes upon optogenetic stimulation (n = 5-8 males per genotype, 3-5 trials per fly, mean ± s.e.m., Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s post hoc test, ns p > 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001). IN1s respond to activation of several sugar-sensing neurons, Gr43a, Gr64c, Gr64e, Gr64f, as well as neurons labelled by TMC >. Supplementary Tables 1, 2 show full experimental genotypes, exact sample sizes, and details of the statistical tests.

a, Representative confocal images of chemosensory and mechanosensory neuron afferents (magenta) and IN1 arbours (green) in the SEZ (scale bars = 50 μm). b, Representative confocal images of chemosensory and mechanosensory neuron afferents (magenta) in the VNC (scale bars = 50 μm). c, Representative confocal images of sensory neuron afferents (magenta) in the foregut (scale bars = 50 μm). Supplementary Tables 1, 2 shows full experimental genotypes and exact sample sizes.

a-c, Representative confocal images of transgenic lines labelling distinct classes of Gr43a neurons (magenta) in the pharynx (a), legs (b), and ENS (c). (scale bars = 25 μm). d, Quantification of Gr43a neurons in flies carrying the indicated transgenes in the CNS, ENS and various chemosensory organs (HCG, hypocerebral ganglion; VNC, ventral nerve cord; LSO, labral sense organ; VCSO, ventral cibarial sense organs; DCSO, dorsal cibarial sense organs). For legs and pharyngeal organs, LSO, VCSO and DCSO, we report the number of neurons unilaterally (n = 3-6 males per genotype, mean ± s.e.m.). Supplementary Tables 1, 2 shows full experimental genotypes and exact sample sizes.

a, Confocal images of Gr43a transgenic flies expressing Chrimson (magenta) in the CNS and ENS (scale bars = 50 μm). b, Confocal images showing localisation of Gr43a neurons (green) and TMC neurons (magenta) in the HCG (scale bars = 25 μm, zoom-in image scale bar=5 μm). No overlap is observed. c, Confocal images showing localisation of Gr43a neurons (green) and Piezo neurons (magenta) in the HCG (scale bars = 50 μm). Some of the Gr43a neurons are co-labelled by Piezo-GAL4 (white arrows). d, Representative confocal images of enteric Gr43a neurons that project to the midgut (magenta). The upper white arrow indicates the midgut surface neuron cell bodies, and the lower white arrow indicates the crop duct (left) (scale bars = 50 μm). Higher magnification boxed area shows the Gr43a projections innervating the midgut (right). e, Cross-sectional images of Gr43a midgut surface neurons in different axes: XY (left) and YZ (right). Arrows indicate the neurites of Gr43a midgut surface neurons (magenta) innervating the gut muscles (blue) (scale bars = 50 μm). f, Area under the curve (AUC) analysis of active Gr43a enteric sensory neuron responses to sucrose ingestion in indicated conditions: AUC (left) and AUC/ingestion duration (right). (n = 8-10 males per condition, mean ± s.e.m. SEM, one-way ANOVA, ns, p > 0.05). g, Normalized (ΔF/F0) GCaMP6s fluorescence in active Gr43a enteric sensory neurons in response to high sucrose (~1 M) ingestion in ~24-h-fasted heterozygous flies (n = 10 males, mean ± s.e.m.). Supplementary Tables 1, 2 show full experimental genotypes, exact sample sizes, and details of the statistical tests.

a, Overview of the split-GAL4 two-photon functional imaging screen. Positive ENs (green), negative ENs (grey), and controls (black) (n = 5-7 males per genotype; five trials per fly; mean ± s.e.m.; Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s post hoc test; p < 0.05-0.0001) (See also Extended Data Fig. 7a-o). c, Representative photo showing enteric sensory neuron imaging during sugar ingestion. d, Confocal images showing expression of GCaMP6s or GCaMP8s in EN> lines (green). Dashed white circles mark ROIs used for fluorescence quantification (scale bars = 50 μm; top). Normalized GCaMP fluorescence (ΔF/F0) in EN> neurons during ingestion of sucrose (~1 M) in ~24-h-fasted flies (n = 4-7 males per genotype; mean ± s.e.m., bottom). e, Confocal images showing colocalization of EN-13 > CD8-RFP (magenta) and Gr43a > CD8-GFP (green) in the HCG. Arrows indicate colabelled enteric sensory neurons (scale bars = 25 μm). f, Cross-sectional (XY and XZ) confocal images showing projections of EN-13 > CD8-RFP (magenta) and Gr43a > CD8-GFP (green) penetrating the foregut lumen (blue) (scale bars = 25 μm). Supplementary Tables 1, 2 show full experimental genotypes, exact sample sizes, and details of the statistical tests.

a, EM reconstruction of putative IN1s (green) together with different classes of GRNs (yellow, pharyngeal GRNs; blue, sweet/water labellar GRNs; red, bitter labellar GRNs) or putative enteric afferents (magenta) in the FAFB connectome. Illustrations are generated in “Natverse” package in R (version 4.3.3) using data from FlyWire and the FAFB14 standard brain mesh. The front view (top) and top view (bottom) are shown. (L, left; R, right; D, dorsal; V, ventral; A, anterior; P, posterior). b-e, Heatmaps showing the connectivity network between IN1s and different classes of GRNs or putative enteric afferents (NC, no path). Heatmaps show the synaptic distance (number of hops) from each neuron to each IN1; connections require ≥5 synapses. IN1s are synaptically closer to putative enteric afferents than pharyngeal or labellar GRNs. A threshold of 5 synapses is used to determine connectivity between pairs of neurons. f, EM reconstruction of putative IN1s (green) with different classes of PER neurons in the FAFB connectome (magenta, second-order PER; yellow, third-order PER; blue, pre-motor PER). The front view (top) and top view (bottom) are shown. (L, left; R, right; D, dorsal; V, ventral; A, anterior; P, posterior). g, Heatmap showing the connectivity network between IN1s and different classes of feeding initiation neurons. Heatmaps show the synaptic distance (number of hops) from each neuron to each IN1; connections require ≥5 synapses. IN1s are at least two synapses away from the PER-triggering second-order, third-order or motor neurons in the SEZ. A threshold of five synapses is used to determine connectivity between pairs of neurons. Neurons with cell bodies in the left hemisphere are labelled with -L, and neurons with cell bodies in the right hemisphere are labelled with -R.

a, Representative heatmap showing the ROI in the crop duct during ingestion (scale bar = 25 μm). b, Normalized food fluorescence in the crop duct before and after ingestion of low (~100 mM) (left) and high (~1 M) (right) sucrose (n = 5 males per condition, mean ± s.e.m.). The sugar stimulus was provided ad libitum. c, Persistence of normalized food fluorescence in the crop duct during the ingestion of low (~100 mM) or high (~1 M) sucrose (n = 5 males per condition, mean ± s.e.m., unpaired two-tailed t-test with Welch’s correction, *p < 0.05). d, A representative image showing the ROI in the oesophagus during ingestion (scale bar=25 μm). e, Normalized food fluorescence in the oesophagus before and after ingestion of low (~100 mM) (left) and high (~1 M) (right) sucrose (n = 5 males per condition, mean ± s.e.m.). The sugar stimulus was provided ad libitum. f, Persistence of normalized food fluorescence in the oesophagus when flies are ingesting low (~100 mM) or high (~1 M) sucrose (n = 5 males per condition, mean ± s.e.m., unpaired two-tailed t-test with Welch’s correction, p = 0.18). g, Normalized food fluorescence in the oesophagus before and after ingestion of high sucrose (~1 M) in flies with indicated genotypes (n = 4-5 males per genotype; mean ± s.e.m.). h, The amount of high sucrose (~1 M) entering the oesophagus is not altered when IN1s are inhibited (n = 4-5 males per genotype; mean ± s.e.m.; one-way ANOVA, p = 0.78). i-j, Normalized food fluorescence in the crop duct of indicated mutant or control flies during ingestion of high sucrose (~1 M) (i), and the persistence of their normalized food fluorescence signal (j). (n = 5-6 males per genotype; mean ± s.e.m., one-way ANOVA, p > 0.05) k-l, Normalized food fluorescence in the oesophagus of indicated mutant or control flies during ingestion of high sucrose (~1 M) (k), and the persistence of their normalized food fluorescence signal (l). (n = 5-6 males per genotype; mean ± s.e.m., one-way ANOVA, p > 0.05). Supplementary Tables 1, 2 show full experimental genotypes, exact sample sizes, and details of the statistical tests.

a-h, EM reconstruction of putative IN1s (cyan, IN1-1; green, IN1-2; blue, IN1-3; red, IN1-4) with their presynaptic inputs (a, c, e, g). Anatomy of the top four presynaptic inputs to IN1-1 (b), IN1-2 (d), IN1-3 (f), or IN1-4 (h) in the FAFB brain dataset is shown. The input neurons are ordered based on their % synaptic input to IN1s. The Codex IDs of input neurons and the percentage of synaptic inputs they provide to IN1s are indicated on top of each panel. A threshold of five synapses is used to determine connectivity between neurons. i, Summary of the synaptic connectivity of IN1s and their major inputs. Arrows indicate the direction of connections (from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurons). Synaptic connections between IN1s are not shown in this graph. Illustrations are generated in the “Natverse” package in R (version 4.3.3) using data from FlyWire and the FAFB14 standard brain mesh.

a-h, EM reconstruction of putative IN1s (cyan, IN1-1; green, IN1-2; violet, IN1-3; red, IN1-4) with their postsynaptic outputs (a, c, e, g). Anatomy of the top four postsynaptic outputs for IN1-1 (b), IN1-2 (d), IN1-3 (f), or IN1-4 (h) in the FAFB brain dataset is shown. The Codex IDs of output neurons and the percentage of synaptic outputs provided by IN1s are shown above each panel. A threshold of five synapses is used to determine connectivity between neurons. i, Summary of the synaptic connectivity of IN1s and their major outputs. Arrows indicate the direction of connections (from presynaptic to postsynaptic neurons). The six neurons (pink) shown in the bottom row (PRW.263, PRW.249, PRW.248, PRW.310, PRW.281, and PRW.274) are the crop-innervating enteric motor neurons (CEM neurons). Synaptic connections between IN1s are not shown in this graph. Illustrations are generated in the “Natverse” package in R (version 4.3.3) using data from FlyWire and the FAFB14 standard brain mesh.

a, IN1s are labelled by IN1>myr-GFP (green, left) and their putative postsynaptic partners revealed by trans-Tango (magenta) in the SEZ (middle) and crop duct (right) (scale bars = 50 μm). b, Representative confocal images of CEM neurons (green) in the male CNS (grey) and their descending projections towards the oesophagus (blue) (scale bars = 25 μm). c, CEM neurons (green) do not send projections to the VNC (grey) (scale bars = 25 μm). d, Confocal images of CEM neurons (green) in the female brain (grey) and their descending projections towards the oesophagus (blue) (scale bars = 25 μm). e, Synaptic terminals of CEM neurons (green) innervating the crop duct (blue) in a female fly. (scale bar = 25 μm). In both conditions, ingested sucrose passes through the foregut, and enteric Gr43a neurons (yellow) detect nutrient arrival in the gut and relay this signal to IN1s (green) in the brain (green arrow). IN1s integrate nutrient/taste input from multiple sources and inhibit CEM neurons (magenta; red lines), which in turn control the crop duct muscles to regulate the routing of ingested food into the crop. f, Under hungry, high-sugar-concentration conditions (~1 M sucrose), the IN1s drive sustained opening of the crop duct, resulting in high crop filling (orange dots indicate ingested sucrose). g, Under fed, low-sugar-concentration conditions (~100 mM sucrose), the same circuit produces only transient opening of the crop duct, resulting in low crop filling. Dashed arrows indicate the path of ingested food through the digestive tract. The differential crop-filling outcomes across conditions reflect the IN1 circuit’s integration of nutrient and metabolic-state information (VNC = ventral nerve cord). The fly schematic is adapted from a prior publication59.

#1030. Germany's celebrated children's author Janosch has died

Bear, Tiger and Tiger-Duck: The author and illustrator Janosch achieved world fame with his heartwarming children's figures. He died at the age of 95.

Janosch, the pen name of German author and illustrator Horst Eckert, won hearts around the world with his warm and simple sense of humor. He charmed children and adults alike with his iconic Tiger, Bear, Tiger-Duck and other animals.

Janosch created more than 150 books, which have been translated into over 30 languages.

His best-selling children's book, "Oh, wie schön ist Panama," translated into English as "The Trip to Panama," was so lucrative that Janosch was able to settle down on the Canary Island of Tenerife in 1980, where he lived together with his wife Ines. The writer and illustrator died peacefully at the age of 95, his publisher Bernhard Feil announced on Wednesday.

Janosch was born as Horst Eckert on March 11, 1931, in Hindenburg (now Zabrze, Poland) in what was then Upper Silesia. After World War II, his family had to flee to Germany.

In 1953, Janosch started studying at the Academy of Art in Munich, thinking that it would be easy to become an artist. He was however dismissed after just a few terms for "lack of talent."

But luckily for his later readers, Janosch did not give up. He continued to work as a freelance artist, soon discovering his second great gift, namely writing.

His first children's book about a horse named Valek was published in 1960.

Although Janosch became famous primarily for his children's books, he also wrote books for adults that focused on his own childhood.

Even though he wrote cheerful books for children, Janosch hardly had any positive memories of his own childhood, as his father was an alcoholic. He was beaten not only by him but also by his mother and grandmother. Raised in a strictly Catholic environment, he was continuously threatened to be punished by God.

Later on, Janosch tried to overcome the burden of his childhood memories by turning to alcohol as well.

He always expressed a great deal of understanding for children, trying to encourage them to stand up for their rights. As a result of his childhood experiences, Janosch did not want to have children himself, and his attitude towards the Catholic Church always remained divided. "As I am a sinner and a heretic, God will let me live a long life so that I can return to the Church," he told his biographer Angela Bajorek.

Janosch's animal figures are endearing but not always well-behaved. They love all kinds of nonsense. But even if they lie to each other or put their own interests first, the true winner at the end of stories is always friendship and solidarity.

Janosch achieved his major breakthrough with "The Trip to Panama," a story about two friends, a little tiger and a bear, who set out to find their paradise in Panama. After touring around in circles, they finally end up where they started out; they realize that their journey was the destination. Janosch received the German Youth Book Prize in 1979 for the work.

Janosch's protagonists have become familiar to generations of children all over the world. They come up over and over again in the various stories carefully illustrated with water colors.

There is the honest lion Hans from the toy chest who fails to catch a nutcracker with his lies. There is Schnuddel and a ridiculous bragger Günter the Box-Frog. And then there is a tiger that collects mushrooms while looking out for his devoted friend, a bear, who always stands up for him even when the tiger temporarily leaves him because of a little pig in one of the stories.

The "Tigerente," literally "Tiger-Duck," a wooden duck on wheels with yellow-brown stripes, appears on numerous pictures by the illustrator. At times, the animal has been tossed into a corner, at times it is hanging from the ceiling, or the Box-Frog pulls it across the drawing.

His iconic figures, especially the Tiger-Duck, have served as motifs on various items, from cups to stamps to jewelry, and even on airplanes. Film adaptations and TV series based on his stories were produced in German and English.

Guests who visited Janosch in Tenerife were impressed by his very modest lifestyle. He always said that hanging around in his hammock doing nothing was what he enjoyed most. And yet Janosch remained very active until the end of his life.

From 2013 to 2019, he wrote a column for the German weekly Die Zeit, taking on the role of Mr. Wondrak, who commented on world affairs. Shortly before his 90th birthday in 2021, the complete collection of his Mr. Wondrak columns were published as a book in German.

Like the protagonists in his stories, Janosch always tried to content himself with few things. As he wrote in one of his books: "He who needs almost nothing, has everything."

This article was originally written in German.

#1026. Liverpool’s expensive attack feast on Palace to leave Sage looking doomed

Crystal Palace are playing this season as if afflicted by a curse. They seem to have made a terrible deal, possibly involving a monkey’s paw. As a result, Pierre Sage’s team were able to defend credibly for around 44 minutes of each half, on one condition: They must switch off completely, at least twice per game.

This being the Premier League, those lapses in concentration are usually punished. A mostly compact performance out of possession briefly became as porous as a bath sponge when Liverpool eased into a 2-0 lead, nine minutes after half-time. Florian Wirtz did not even need to finish cleanly to score his first Premier League goal of the season, striding on to an unopposed low cross from Bradley Barcola and killing the match as a contest.

Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz combine to put Liverpool 2-0 up! 🔴 https://t.co/F6sw33FkYZ

Major signings need to lay down a marker when arriving at Liverpool. Barcola has his hat-trick at LASK in the Champions League, but we are still waiting for a stirring big-match-defining contribution from him since his summer arrival. Arguably the same could be said for Wirtz, nearly 18 months since he joined.

Neither left Selhurst Park looking like the world-beaters they did occasionally for their previous clubs. Still, one misfiring attacker creating a goal for another represents progress and all great partnerships must start somewhere. Lennon and McCartney would improve after 1958’s Too Bad About Sorrows.

If there was ever a place for the least-productive expensively assembled attacking group in the league to find form it was surely south London on this Sunday lunchtime. Liverpool came in with two defeats in their previous two but, European trophy aside, it has been a lousy 2026 for Palace.

They have the most defeats of any ever-present Premier League team and began (and ended) the weekend with the worst defensive record. They have conceded twice as many goals from headers as any other team. Even their most loyal fan group has disbanded.

Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring in gut-punching fashion, after a series of Palace near-misses. Chairman Steve Parish rubbed his face in the directors’ box, in the style of peak-stress era Guardiola. None of this looked good for Sage, who appears on the brink of dismissal, with Thomas Frank his most likely replacement.

Asked if he expected to remain in his job on the other side of the international break Sage said he deemed his prospects “better than you, I think”.

“We deserved better today,” the Frenchman said. “But football is not about what you deserve it is about how efficient you are and today we had a lack of efficiency”.

Counter-intuitively, it was Palace’s flashes of promise which suggested the Frenchman might be doomed. There is enough to work with here, and plenty going marginally against Palace to suggest a change in leadership might prompt a turnaround, however unfair it would be on their manager. Yéremy Pino hit the bar, Jorgen Strand Larsen had his composed close-range goal struck from the record by VAR, Daichi Kamada stung Alisson Becker’s palms and the Brazilian saved well again from Adam Wharton’s feathered header.

Another header conceded.

#1023. BMW reports lower Q3 earnings as China woes mount

BMW reports a drop in profits in the July to September quarter amid fierce competition from China.

German carmaker BMW reported a nearly 15% drop in third-quarter net profit on Wednesday, as competition from China shakes the global car industry.

Net profit for the third quarter fell to 1.45 billion euros ($1.61 billion), while sales fell nearly 6% to 30.45 billion euros, BMW said.

The main cause of the decline was BMW's poor business in China. Although the company sold more cars in the US and Europe compared to the same period last year, this could only partially offset the decline in China.

BMW's car deliveries in China, which were already at their lowest level since 2017 last year, fell 24.8% in the quarter and consequently dragged global deliveries down by 6.3.

CEO Milan Nedeljkovic said his company would "specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures."

BMW on Tuesday also lowered its outlook for the current year, citing the faster-than-planned implementation of restructuring measures that includes 8,000 layoffs in its home market.

German carmakers have been struggling to compete with their Chinese counterparts in the electric vehicle market,  resulting in cost-cutting measures.

Volkswagen, the world's second-largest carmaker, is battling mounting competition from falling demand in its core Chinese market.

BMW, and its industry heavyweight peers, Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, have announced plans to scale back production and reduce costs.

On the other hand, German auto parts supplier Schaeffler announced on Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe, by 2028.

According to the company statement, three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany.

German automotive supplier Bosch, the world's biggest, announced last year that it would cut 13,000 jobs, mostly in its auto division.

#1019. Harry Potter films turns 25 ahead of new TV series' release

In 2001, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" hit cinemas and took the world by storm. Today, anticipation for the new series is high, but its creator, J.K. Rowling, remains a controversial figure.

On November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").

"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.

Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour."

The crowds showed just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.

The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.

About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.

Today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.

At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.

With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.

For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.

But in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an issue Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.

In an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.

Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.

The controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

Others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.

The "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.

Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been announced, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.

The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO says, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the new production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently said she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.

This article was originally written in German.

Accessories complete the set, with an ABC CAMO duffle bag and a BABY MILO shoulder bag rounding out the collection.

Fronted by Real Madrid and Brazil legend Marcelo, known for his flair on and off the pitch, the 'adidas x BAPE' football collection is a truly global statement piece, appealing to fashion fans and football enthusiasts from Asia to the Americas and Europe.

The collection drops September 6th via Confirmed, adidas.com, select adidas retail partners, BAPE.com, and BAPE STORE locations worldwide.

#1015. Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Intratumoural heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic and phenotypic diversity, is pervasive in cancer and a fundamental barrier to curative treatment1,2. How these heterogeneous cell states emerge and co-evolve within tumours remains poorly understood. Here we develop a deep-learning framework that quantifies colorectal cancer tissue architecture and nuclear morphology at subcellular resolution to predict patient outcome. Integrating this with spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids, we identify a co-evolutionary relationship between tumour architecture and cancer cell states. We identify architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer that drive cell state diversification by promoting distinct cancer stem cell programmes. Specifically, tissue fragmentation generates compressive forces that activate YAP, suppressing classical stem cell programmes and inducing fetal/regenerative stem cell states that initially manifest as hybrid states with features of partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Subsequent tumour–stroma communication through TGFβ diversifies these into distinct stem cell and EMT states. Reciprocally, β-catenin activity tunes tumour cell responsiveness to architectural cues. Collectively, this work identifies a feedforward loop between cell states and tissue architecture that drives cancer heterogeneity and cell state diversification. Machine-learning-based analyses harness this co-dependency, independently of mutational status or cancer stage, to predict patient outcome.

Most cancers comprise genetically, epigenetically and phenotypically diverse cell states within a variable stroma1,2. A substantial proportion of this heterogeneity arises independently of somatic mutations3 and associates with poor prognosis by diversifying cell states that evade therapy1,2. Whether tissue organization and cell state heterogeneity co-evolve, and how cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic mechanisms interact to drive tumour progression, remain unresolved.

The intestinal epithelium is sustained by a resident adult stem cell (SC) pool4, which also gives rise to and drives colorectal cancer (CRC). During CRC progression, adult SC signatures are depleted while fetal-like/regenerative programmes, which are otherwise present only during development or tissue damage, re-emerge and expand further after metastasis or treatment5,6,7. This plasticity generates extensive heterogeneity and limits therapy responsiveness. Metastatic behaviour requires loss of canonical colonic SC identity, activation of TGFβ and YAP, and acquisition of a fetal-like SC state5,6,7,8.

Genetic drivers of CRC, including BRAF and KRAS mutations and microsatellite instability (MSI), are well established9, but phenotypic plasticity can also arise through epigenetic and transcriptional reprogramming10,11. CRC progression also involves microenvironmental remodelling, including immune infiltration and signalling from cancer-associated fibroblasts12,13,14, together with altered tissue mechanics such as increased extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffness and elevated interstitial pressure15,16. These changes are known to alter cell states and promote aggression17,18,19,20. Finally, nuclear shape abnormalities serve as diagnostic indicators of cancer21,22, suggesting that phenotypic heterogeneity is coupled to nuclear organization23,24,25,26. However, how nuclear architecture, tissue organization and cellular heterogeneity are related remains poorly understood.

Here we develop a machine-learning-based image analysis framework to quantify CRC architecture and nuclear morphology, and find that both are highly prognostic independently of mutational status or disease stage. Integrating spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids reveals that distinct tumour architectures associate with specific nuclear morphologies and cell state programmes, and that architecture and phenotypic plasticity co-evolve within individual patients. Mechanistically, tumour fragmentation and associated compressive stress promote transition of LGR5-positive SCs to an ANXA1-positive fetal-like state through YAP, whereas ECM composition and stromal TGFβ signalling promote EMT. These findings reveal a feedforward loop between tissue architecture, nuclear shape and cell state diversification that drives poor outcome in CRC.

To investigate the relationship between nuclear morphology, tissue architecture and disease outcome, we obtained pathologist-curated tumour microarrays (TMAs) from 1,342 patients with CRC with complete clinical information (Extended Data Fig. 1a). TMA punches were taken from primary tumour resection specimens at paired tumour core (CT; 1,834 cores) and invasive margin (IM; 1,502 cores) locations (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1b). The slides were stained for the epithelial marker pan-cadherin (pan-EPI) to identify tumour cell boundaries and to separate tumour from stroma, and with DAPI to mark all nuclei (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1c). Nuclei were segmented at single-cell resolution27 (over 25 million cells) to derive quantitative descriptors of nuclear shape, size and deformation (Fig. 1b). Patients with MSI and microsatellite-stable (MSS) patients were analysed separately.

The dashed line demarcates tumour (T) and stroma (S). Scale bars, 500 µm (top) and 25 µm (bottom). b, Schematic of nuclear morphometry parameters extracted from single-cell nuclear segmentation. Scale bars, 5 μm.  c, Pearson correlation matrix of nuclear morphometry features across all single cells from the CT and IM. d, Univariate Cox proportional hazard analysis of patient-averaged nuclear morphometrics for disease-specific survival in MSS patients. The x axis shows the log hazard ratio with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the CT (blue; n = 773 patients) and IM (pink; n = 484 patients). A patient is counted in a compartment only when that compartment has a nuclear-morphometry average and a survival time. Nuclear circularity is the strongest indicator of poor survival. P values were calculated using Wald tests. e, Schematic of the tumour architecture classification pipeline. TMA cores with homogeneous architecture were used to train a U-Net and generate feature embeddings (blue, solid (sol.); yellow, glandular (gland.); red, fragmented (frag.)).
