#942. WSL makes agreement with clubs to avoid gambling sponsors

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Clubs have agreed to prioritise sponsorship deals with companies in other industries

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

WSL Football, the organisation responsible for operating the top two tiers of women’s football in the UK, has reached an agreement in principle for its clubs not to make sponsorship deals with betting companies.

Instead, the organisation has agreed to pursue sponsorship deals with brands from different industries, reports The Athletic. The outlet states that six additional sponsorship opportunities were made available ahead of the 2024/25 season, and these were filled by Apple, Airbnb, British Gas, Mercedes, Tesco and WTW.

While the agreement applies to WSL Football’s own commercial partnerships, it does not stop individual WSL or WSL2 clubs from signing sponsorship deals with gambling companies.

Rather, it sets a different direction for WSL Football’s league-level partnerships, giving the leagues the chance to shape their own commercial future. The organisation wants to continue aiding the growth of the women’s domestic game, while combating issues such as player welfare, gambling-related online abuse and fluctuating attendances.

The changes also come at a time when English football is starting to take a wider look at gambling and related sponsorships. At the start of this season, the Premier League’s voluntary ban on betting sponsors appearing on the front of match-day shirts came into effect, while the Premier League, EFL, FA and WSL also introduced a Code of Conduct for gambling-related sponsorship agreements in 2024.

Nevertheless, betting companies still feature prominently among sponsors at clubs throughout the top divisions in the men’s game, with Betway signing a deal with Manchester United and clubs such as Leeds and Nottingham Forest also agreeing new deals over the summer.

#940. Norway's ice hockey team says Russia replacing it at World Juniors

The wrangling over Russia's return to international ice hockey continues, with Norway saying it has been kicked out of the next major tournament to accommodate Russia. Switzerland has joined a "boycott."

With just weeks to go until the start of the 2027 World Junior Championship, it remains unclear who will be the 10th, and final, participant. This comes after the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) had said it had been removed from the tournament so that Russia could take part.

The move, which has yet to be publicly announced by the IIHF, comes in apparent response to the Court of Arbitration (CAS) ruling in late October, which ordered it to allow Russia to return to international play. The World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the CAS decision.

The IIHF barred Russia and Belarus from international play shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

In a statement issued Saturday, the IIHF said it was "taking the necessary steps required by the CAS ruling and reviewing what conditions would need to be met to safeguard our Championships, protect the organization's financial stability and secure the long-term future of international ice hockey."

As of Monday, the IIHF website still listed Norway as one of the participants in the World Juniors, which is to be hosted by Edmonton and Red Deer, Alberta, beginning on December 26. But Swiss Ice Hockey has responded to Norway's statement, saying its team would not face Russia at the World Juniors — as would be the case if it replaces Norway in the schedule.

However, it's far from certain that Russia will actually be able to ice a team in the tournament, as just last week, the Canadian prime minister ruled out the possibility.

"While Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal, unjustified ​war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," said Mark Carney.

"So, ​if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there."

How this circle could be squared is unclear. Carney's pledge, coupled with the stated refusal by Finland, Sweden, Switzerland and others to face Russia in an international tournament, appears to have given the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association (NIHF) hope that its team could still play in the upcoming tournament. Several long-time corporate sponsors have also threatened to pull out if Russia is allowed to compete.

"This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada in December," said NIHF General Secretary Petter Salsten.

"The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association is awaiting further information from the IIHF in the coming days."

Meanwhile, the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) is still in discussions with the government in Berlin and the IIHF about how to proceed — or not — with hosting the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in May.

"We intend to host the world championship in Germany next year, and I am very optimistic that we will succeed in doing so," DEB chairman Frank H. Lutz told German broadcaster MagentaSport on Saturday.

While he acknowledged the IIHF's CAS-ordered requirement to include Russia and reiterated the DEB's rejection of the court ruling, he provided no indication as to how this obstacle could be overcome.

Lutz, who said he would be in Berlin for more consultations this week, had previously said handing back Germany's hosting rights was a possibility — if only as a last resort.

On Friday, government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said Berlin supports the DEB's efforts to find a solution.

"However, given the boycotts that would follow Russia's readmission, that would effectively be impossible. For this reason, we intend to explore, through dialogue, how we can still ensure the tournament takes place."

Asked at the same press conference whether Germany could issue visas to a Russian team for the tournament, a Foreign Ministry spokesman indicated that this would be difficult under restrictions currently in place.

"At a time when Russia is waging a war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no 'normalcy' — and we will certainly not pretend that there is," said spokesperson Martin Giese.

However, he did not categorically rule out the possibility.

It has been suggested that government officials could be choosing their words carefully out of concern for Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees who are bidding to host an Olympic Games — like the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) — to follow its lead.

Asked whether the debate over Russia's possible involvement in a hockey tournament could affect Munich's chances, government spokesman Kornelius said he didn't wish to "speculate on implications."

Still, with the IOC set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process, one has to think that the issue could hardly have come up at a more inopportune time for the DOSB.

#938. How Man United fans revolted against the Glazers to create their own football club

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Play the viral 442GOALS game and build an XI of Premier League legends!

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Fantastic football content straight to your inbox! From the latest transfer news, quizzes, videos, features and interviews with the biggest names in the game, plus lots more.

Sign up to our FREE live football newsletter, tracking all of the biggest games available to watch on the device of your choice. Never miss a kick-off!

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Horrified at the Glazer family’s impending takeover two decades ago, a group of Manchester United fans went to church. FC United was their divine inspiration, a phoenix club born at the heart of the community

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Revolution can spark in the most unlikely places. John Lennon knew that. The former Beatle and wife Yoko Ono needed only an Amsterdam hotel room to stage their 1969 protest over the Vietnam War. Lennon’s decision to start a revolution from his bed would later be immortalised in the lyrics of Oasis’ Imagine pastiche Don’t Look Back in Anger.

Fully 36 years after that legendary ‘bed-in’, a group of football supporters chose an equally unlikely venue to kick-start their own revolution. Outraged by a hostile takeover of their beloved Manchester United, and fed up with where football appeared to be heading in general, they convened in May 2005 to discuss a notion that would send shockwaves through the English game. The meeting place: Methodist Central Hall in Manchester’s Northern Quarter.

“There was a buzz in the air,” explains Jules Spencer, a lifelong Manchester United fan who attended the event and had taken part in other protests. “We’d fought against change before, including Rupert Murdoch’s attempted takeover. But this was the final straw.”

Back in 1999, the United Kingdom’s Competition Commission had blocked Murdoch and BSkyB’s £625 million bid for Manchester United, the government’s reasoning that the acquisition would have “hurt competition in the broadcast industry and the quality of British football”. The next major power grab would not be so easily thwarted, though.

Malcolm Glazer, an American business tycoon and owner of NFL franchise the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, had first bought nearly three per cent of Manchester United in March 2003. Through a series of incremental buyouts, that stake neared 30 per cent by October 2004 – a threshold above which Glazer would have to launch a formal takeover bid.

Businessmen muscling into football was nothing new, but as the takeover drew nearer supporters became increasingly concerned. Most of the capital used by Glazer to buy the club would come in the form of loans, the majority of which were secured against the club’s assets, incurring average interest payments of more than £46m per annum.

“It was,” lifelong Red Devils fan Paul Hurst says, “absolutely scandalous.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In February 2005, hundreds of United fans protested outside Old Trafford, with some hanging an effigy of Glazer. That month, the idea for a breakaway club was first mooted by now defunct fanzine Red Issue.

“As the spectre of Malcolm Glazer looms ever larger, the question has been increasingly asked: ‘What would you do if he did take over?’” they penned. “What if you could give up supporting Glazer’s company without giving up United?

“Back in the days of the Murdoch campaign, an evacuation plan was drawn up, detailing the blueprint for the formation of a new Manchester United, one which spurned the commercialism and tackiness of the modern game, and was controlled and run by the fans. With United again under threat, those plans have been resurrected. With a working name of ‘FC United’, the logistics of the operation to set up a new Manchester United has been looked into.”

The article outlined the bold ambition. “We would await regime change, while aiding all attempts to undermine the illegitimate occupation,” it continued. “When Glazer is defeated, FC United will be happy to return to Old Trafford and merge with ‘the franchise’ on condition that the supporters’ trust maintains full ownership of the football club and the unified Manchester United take over the higher league position of FC United. Viva la revolucion.”

Three months later, Glazer completed his takeover, reaching the 75 per cent threshold required to end the club’s public limited company (PLC) status and delist from the London Stock Exchange.

It prompted fans to assemble and discuss a new club at Methodist Central Hall, complete with Styrofoam cups of tea in hand, surrounded by murals of Bible scenes and psalms.

“I’d taken part in the protests against the Glazers, along with so many others,” says Hurst, who was at that meeting. “Many of us pledged not to give the club one penny more while Glazer owned it. We wouldn’t be paying off his debts.”

“It wasn’t about switching off our allegiance to Manchester United – that would never go,” remembers Spencer. “It was about letting Manchester United and the Glazers know that we wouldn’t stand idly by and allow this to happen. If necessary, we were willing to put our money towards something else instead, something positive to be proud of.”

Red Issue editor John-Paul O’Neill organised the new movement, backed by a steering committee. “It was drawn from across the fanbase, from official fan groups to business people and those with marketing and communications expertise,” says team member Spencer. “We held more meetings, with around 1,500 people joining at Manchester’s Apollo theatre. Not everybody was convinced, but they came along to hear what we had to say. Momentum began to build and some fans started to pledge their United season ticket money to help us get off the ground. It was so exciting.”

Preparations included a visit from Kris Stewart, chairman of AFC Wimbledon, founded three years earlier. “His insight was invaluable,” recalls Spencer. “We didn’t really know what we were doing at that stage. He told us we were in for a lot of hard work and that a lot would go wrong, but it’d be totally worth it if we pulled it off. He remained a valued sounding board in the months to come.”

Time was of the essence. The new club had to be set up and registered well before the new 2005-06 season, already less than two months away. Failing to do so would risk losing momentum. They didn’t even have a name.

The FA vetoed ‘FC United’ for being too generic, so those who’d pledged money were asked to vote on a different name. Manchester Central and Newton Heath United were discarded as options – in June, ‘FC United of Manchester’ got the nod and joined the 10th-tier North West Counties Division Two. While it wasn’t their official moniker, many called them FC United anyway

There was still the not insignificant issue of finding some players. Some 900 applications were whittled down to 200 trialists, from which Karl Marginson, the club’s inaugural manager, would select a squad of 17.

“The standard of the trialists was very strong and we put together a team I felt capable of challenging for the title in our first campaign,” he tells FFT now.

How did the manager get the gig? “It was between me and one other bloke, and he was a Scouser,” Marginson, a born-and-bred Manc chuckles. “I was 34 – I’d been an assistant at Flixton, so not had a proper manager’s job before, but I knew the league well.

“I’d been a Manchester United fan all my life and didn’t like where the original club was heading. I didn’t think my own kids would be able to afford to go when they were old enough, the way I had as a teenager, and that was so wrong. The new club was important and I think they could see what it meant to me as well. I was young and ambitious – the idea of taking charge of a totally new club appealed to me.”

Their first match was a drab 0-0 draw at Leigh RMI. The pre-season friendly was watched by more than 2,500 fans, TV crews and national journalists. “It was magnificent and bonkers at the same time,” says Marginson. “There was a party atmosphere in the air, even for such a terrible game. I couldn’t believe what I’d let myself in for.”

A similar-sized crowd flocked to FC United’s first competitive match, a 5-2 victory at Leek County School Old Boys, whose ground was used to hosting fans by the dozen, not the thousand. Home matches, staged at Bury’s Gigg Lane as part of a long-term groundsharing deal, delivered gates as large as 6,000 during a season that consistently smashed the league’s attendance records.

“It was incredible to see,” reminisces future board member Hurst. “The level of football was very different to what we’d been used to, nine divisions higher in the Premier League, but the sense of community more than made up for it.”

The matchday mood wasn’t always positive, though. Throughout the club’s formation, a small yet vocal group of Manchester United supporters had railed against the movement, branding those involved traitors. Tensions flared during a game against Salford City. “The fixture had to be switched to Salford’s rugby league ground due to the expected crowd,” explains Hurst.

“Lots of Manchester United fans bought tickets to protest against us, which was ironic. They had some banners calling us turncoats and all the rest of it. It got quite unpleasant.”

Even Sir Alex Ferguson weighed in on the new club, labelling the movement “a shame” and questioning whether those involved were really proper Red Devils to begin with.

“Listen, we could all understand the criticism to a certain degree,” continues Hurst. “The new club was divisive, even within families and friendship circles.

“There were those that saw it as the genuine protest movement it was – a necessary act of defiance – and others who saw us as Judases who turned our back on the club in its hour of need. That was never the case.

“Many of us are passionate Manchester United supporters. We just didn’t want to fund Glazer’s debts by going to games. Thankfully, a lot of that hatred has died down since.”

On-field headlines were positive. The Red Rebels swept to the Division Two title in their first season, finishing eight points clear of Marginson’s former club Flixton. “A fantastic achievement,” he says. “It was important to show that we were a club that meant business in footballing terms as well, beyond the protest club element.”

They were far from done. FC United won promotion again in their second campaign, then another in their third to reach the Northern Premier Division, two levels below the National League and three from the EFL.

A fourth promotion was squandered in 2010-11, courtesy of a play-off final defeat to Colwyn Bay. Earlier in that season, FC United had advanced to the FA Cup first round for the first time, then won at League One Rochdale to set up a second round showdown at Brighton, who would go on to win the third tier that term.

The 10-man Red Rebels even led at the Withdean Stadium, before Mauricio Taricco’s late equaliser earned Gus Poyet’s Seagulls a replay they would win 4-0 at Gigg Lane. The 6,900 gate that night was more than 1,500 higher than the first encounter in East Sussex.

Further play-off defeats followed in 2012, 2013 and 2014. “I definitely felt the pressure to win matches and keep taking the football club forward,” says Marginson. “I was still inexperienced and we were getting huge attendances to every game.

“We had one of the bigger budgets in those leagues and supporters expected a lot. I already drank alcohol, but I’d be lying if I said I didn’t lean into that a bit more to help cope.”

Promotion eventually came in 2015 – not only did FC United secure a fifth successive top-six finish, this time they won the league, during a campaign in which they groundshared with Curzon Ashton and Stalybridge Celtic. “It was an epic achievement,” says Marginson with pride. “The club stuck by me and we got there in the end.”

The timing couldn’t have been better, with a new 4,700-capacity home all of their own ready to move into.

“Gigg Lane served us incredibly well, but financially it made more sense for us to have somewhere permanent,” says director Hurst. “We scouted out a number of sites before the council let us build a new stadium in Moston.”

Located just four miles north-east of Manchester city centre, Broadhurst Park cost £6.5m and hosted its first match, a friendly against Benfica B, on May 29 that year – the same date on which Manchester United beat Benfica in the 1968 European Cup Final. “It felt like a massive step for us,” adds Spencer. “A place to stand with our friends, our sons and daughters, and call home.”

FC United finished a respectable 13th in the National League North on two occasions, but a tough start to 2017-18 resulted in Marginson’s exit. “If you’d have told me when I first took the job that I’d still have been there all those years later, I’d have said, ‘No chance’,” he says, reflecting on 12 years in charge. “I think back to the young man I was when I became manager – it’s a world apart. I couldn’t have done the job had I been older. It needed youth and energy from the off. Eventually, I ran out.”

A new injection arrived in the form of striker Tom Greaves – the club’s all-time top scorer – who stepped up to a player-manager role. He steered the club to survival but departed after a poor start to the next campaign, to be replaced by Neil Reynolds. He, though, couldn’t turn the tide, with FC United relegated back to the Northern Premier Division. COVID annulled 2019-20 when they were sat second and set for the play-offs again – five years on, they’re yet to return to the sixth tier of the pyramid.

Not that it’s all been doom and gloom. Later in 2020, FC United reached the FA Cup first round for the third time, facing League One Doncaster Rovers in front of the live TV cameras. A year after that, they were invited to participate in the inaugural Fenix Trophy, a tournament contested by a selection of unusual non-league sides from across Europe. The Mancunians travelled to face AKS Zly in Warsaw, and Brera in Milan, going on to beat Prague Raptors in the final in the Italian city of Rimini.

In 2022-23, they again reached the latter stages of the competition, losing a semi to BK Skjold of Denmark but then beating Brera at Milan’s San Siro, no less. Last season, after matches in Krakow and Paris, they won the cup for a second time, defeating Prague Raptors in the final once more, on the shores of Lake Garda on this occasion.

“I certainly didn’t envisage leading my team-mates out at San Siro when I first joined,” says club captain Charlie Ennis, who arrived in the summer of 2019. “Getting changed in Milan’s dressing room and walking out onto that iconic pitch – it still gives me goosebumps now. We’ve been very lucky to be a part of the competition, travelling across Europe. It’s been one of the highlights of my career.”

Ennis, now 34, is another who didn’t expect to stay as long as he has. “I was no spring chicken when I signed,” he jokes. “But I’m a local lad and, short of playing for Manchester United, who I grew up supporting, there’s nowhere else I’d rather be. We get big crowds, play at a fantastic ground and this club means so much to people. The best years are yet to come.”

The man tasked with leading them into the next era is gaffer Mark Beesley, who replaced Reynolds in September after resigning from Warrington Town. His squad includes 38-year-old former Reading and Bolton forward Adam Le Fondre, a lifelong Manchester United fan who spoke of semi-fulfilling a dream when signing from Scottish Premiership side Hibernian last summer.

Whatever the future holds, FC United can already look back on the past two decades with enormous pride. “It’s been a lot of hard work, but I wouldn’t have changed it for the world,” director Hurst tells FFT now. “You look over at Manchester United, what continues to happen at the club with its ownership, and you’d be hard pressed to say we were wrong to do this. We’ve given local football fans a positive alternative.”

Manchester United are still majority-owned by the Glazers. Malcolm passed the reins to his sons before his death in 2014. Since the family took charge, it’s estimated the club has paid out more than £750m in interest fees on loan repayments alone. Debts remain high, while on-field success has steadily declined since Ferguson’s retirement. Ineos impresario Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s £1bn investment for a 27.7 per cent stake has rekindled neither success nor spirit.

“We want more than anything for that to change, for the Glazers to sell up, and for Manchester United to become a well-run club again,” says Spencer. “I’m still a Manchester United fan. I was jumping for joy when we beat City in last season’s FA Cup final. But as long as the Glazers are still there, I can’t be.”

Until that day, and long after, Spencer and his fellow rebels will be found at Broadhurst Park. “I come here with my sons and it’s a special feeling,” he says. “It’s something positive that we can all share as a community. I look back at that meeting at the church hall all those years ago and can’t help but laugh at how far we’ve come since. We made the right decision.

Ed is a staff writer at FourFourTwo, working across the magazine and website. A German speaker, he’s been working as a football reporter in Berlin since 2015, predominantly covering the Bundesliga and Germany's national team. Favourite FFT features include an exclusive interview with Jude Bellingham following the youngster’s move to Borussia Dortmund in 2020, a history of the Berlin Derby since the fall of the Wall and a celebration of Kevin Keegan’s playing career.

The Celtic great moved south of the border in 1977

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When Kenny Dalglish arrived at Liverpool from Celtic in 1977, he arrived as a 26-year-old, just entering his peak years.

Signed as a replacement for Hamburg-bound Kop icon Kevin Keegan, Dalglish eclipsed even King Kev’s achievements in Reds shirt over the next decade and a half.

But the Scot’s move to Anfield almost happened a decade earlier, when he was still a teenager.

“Myself and another boy were invited for trials with Liverpool when I was a teenager,” Dalglish tells FourFourTwo. “We played a game, then I was asked to go back for a couple of weeks.

“Shanks [Billy Shankly] was there, I played a game and they said. ‘We'd like to sign you.' I thought, ‘It's a bit far from Glasgow…' I knew that Liverpool was a great club, I just thought it was too far away for a 15-year-old boy going down there by himself.”

Dalglish would go on to become a Celtic great, winning four Scottish league titles and four Scottish Cups before Liverpool came knocking again.

“Then in 1977, when I was 26, I'd been in South America for World Cup warm-ups with Scotland, because the World Cup was going to be in Argentina the next year,” he recalls.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I came home, Celtic were going to Australia and I said to the manager, ‘I don't want to go.' Jock Stein said, ‘Go home and think about it.'

“I told him, ‘I have thought about it', and by the way, for me to stand up to him like that, I was terrified! I stayed at Celtic Park and trained with the reserves.

What followed next was a clear sign that Stein was preparing for life without his star player.

“When the first team came back, I played a couple of pre-season games, one at Dunfermline. We were in the dressing room, ready to go out and I was captain, but Big Jock threw the ball at one of the other players and said, ‘On you go, you take them out.'

“The rest of them were all saying to me, ‘Oh… where are *you* going?' I said, ‘I don't know!' “After the game, I dropped into my father-in-law's pub on the way home. Big Jock phoned the pub and said, ‘Right, do you still want to go?' I said, ‘Aye, boss.' He said, ‘Get yourself up here, there are two people who want to talk to you.'

“It was about 10.30pm – Bob Paisley and the chairman of Liverpool were there. About five minutes later, everything was agreed.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#936. Succumbing to certainty is a failure in science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Dom Byrne is a freelance radio and podcast producer based in Brighton, UK.

Scientists should resist political pressure to provide certainty when the evidence suggests otherwise, says Andy Stirling.Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript

Science’s greatest failure is not getting things wrong, but by sometimes pretending that there is more certainty than there really is, says social scientist Andy Stirling.

This can happen, he says, when researchers face political pressure to provide a single, definitive answer, when the evidence is far more complex.

In the final episode of a six-part podcast series about failure in science, Stirling, an emeritus professor at the University of Sussex in Brighton, UK, draws on examples from climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic, environmental campaigns and energy policy.

“In those areas, science just does not convey the degree of uncertainty and of variability and of how many potentially viable options are being cut out when you just give one clear answer,” he says. “It thinks it’s helping society by just giving one picture of the truth. And in fact, it’s undermining both itself and democracy when it does that.”

Stirling, whose research includes science and technology policy and environmental politics, says that on occasions politicians have almost literally hidden behind scientists on a podium, who have relied on their authority and expertise to protect them.

Earlier this year, Stirling spoke at a one-day conference on failure in science, with a focus on careers and innovation. It was held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03837-y

Well, my failure is to take my own advice.

The thing I want to say here, I, you know, talk the talk.

I’m big on talking the talk, but walking the walk is tricky.

That’s social scientist Professor Andy Stirling at the opening session of the Failure in Science conference, held at Imperial College London in April 2026.

It’s why I’m so motivated. I’ll create a false frisson of expectation.

It’s why I’m so motivated to say what I’m going to say in this panel that it is so difficult.

Up until now, in this series, we’ve talked about individual scientists seeing failure come their way.

And we’ve talked about science institutions, universities, trying to get good at allowing failure as part and parcel of science.

But as a social scientist peering at science through that lens, Professor Stirling takes this a step further.

I’m trying to contribute with many others to a move towards making it okay to speak about how the results we get in science are never, even when we are massively successful, never mind when we’re failing.

They are never as singular, and unambiguous, and definitive as our disciplines, our superiors, and policymakers force us to pretend.

If science is supposed to exist for the betterment of humanity, is it actually doing a good job?

Does science fail sometimes or often when it heads out into society?

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

In episode six, we explore how the very project of science sometimes fails our society, and we discuss how it could adapt to better serve its citizens.

We’re asking, how can good science and good science policy benefit from admitting that sometimes we don’t really know?

What we’re discussing here, of course, is science and democracy, where we like to believe everyone has their say.

Well, my name’s Andy Stirling, and I’m a professor at the University of Sussex, and visiting or honorary at UCL and Leiden.

Given that my topic is on how science functions in society, one of my best candidates, I think, for a failure is just being so slow to realize how power works around science.

I’ve spent years, you know, chipping in in modest ways on advisory processes, advisory committees on this and that topic because of the nature of the work I do, and it took me a long time to realize just how powerful the forces are that pressurize science into giving certain kinds of answers, or not asking certain kinds of questions.

Those forces are much more powerful than I had thought at the beginning. Even though I thought of myself quite hard-nosed, I’ve really been quite surprised.

Sure, yeah. Well, look, it was a fantastic conference all around different aspects of failure, and that was in the context of a lot of people talking really eloquently about failure within science, and actually how science can benefit and people can benefit from failure.

So that was a context for me picking up that science itself has, in an important sense, failed itself and society.

And in saying that, I absolutely didn’t say it out of a spirit of being critical of science.

It’s because I am so enthusiastic. I regard science as so precious that the disappointment, as it were, of that is all the more acute when you value science in society.

And I said it because, in a nutshell, I think science fails to communicate the most important thing about itself to society, and that matters because the times in which people are most listening to science is when there’s some kind of crisis about climate, about some sort of technology that’s causing a risk, about what to do with future innovation.

So on those areas, science just does not convey the degree of uncertainty and of variability and of how many potentially viable options are being cut out when you just give one clear answer.

It thinks it’s helping society by just giving one picture of the truth.

And in fact, it’s undermining both itself and democracy when it does that.

You’ll probably want to unpack what I mean by all that, but that’s the nutshell.

So yeah, I think it is useful to see science as a social movement. That’s not the only way to see it. There’s all kinds of different views. It’s in the spirit of my, what I’m trying to say that there are different ways of viewing this one thing.

But all the more important because it gets neglected.

Science is very often as much by critics sometimes as by its protagonists, put forward in any given area as being some objective source of authority, a definitive authority.

And even if uncertainties are acknowledged, there’s a kind of disembodied, detached idea of scientific expertise.

And one can understand that. I mean, I say this in the spirit of really respecting how amazing the transcendent kind of progress can be in areas by really applying scientific method.

But we tend to forget that science is itself located in society.

So the kinds of questions that it asks, the kinds of resources that are applied, the kinds of attitudes that it takes when it’s challenged or when it’s trying to influence, is very human, subject to all kinds of interest.

I mean, how often do scientists display enormous enthusiasm about their particular field, often their particular technology?

They’re highly partisan. It comes with the ability to be highly critical. It doesn’t, it’s not separate.

There’s certain questions won’t be asked for many years unless you get different disciplines together, and then they’ll ask each other more difficult questions. But often they won’t even talk to each other.

So yeah, it’s a social movement. It’s a collection of social movements, and by that I mean, I mean it’s got all kinds of institutions and organizations and cultures in it.

But maybe a good way to illustrate this is the Royal Society, one of the first in the modern idea of science in the world.

Their motto in the 17th century was nullius in verba. Not on anyone’s word, not on authority.

And it is deliciously ironic when you see now these enormous reports on nuclear or geoengineering or gene editing being slapped down on the table with the motto nullius in verba, when in fact it is being used as a source of authority.

But the the foundation of science, it was a reaction to doctrinal assertions from the monarchy or from the church.

And scientists were saying we want to argue about it. We want to have experiments. We want to have analysis. We want to have reasoned arguments about how you can draw different conclusions.

And of course, in the beginning, that was highly exclusive. It was old white males.

But nonetheless, the principle was you should be able to argue with each other, irrespective of your authority.

And now, I’m afraid, science is often a little bit seduced by power and privilege. It gets locked into patronage networks so that, you know, it gets rewarded, and too often it sees itself as a source of authority rather than a source of questions.

When we say with climate change, what does the, what does, do what the science says.

There are a lot of activists come out with banners saying that, but also you know chief scientists often find themselves saying something similar.

And you can’t because the science says nothing without values and interests to help frame it.

There’s nothing about evidence and data in the climate area as anywhere else that actually compels you to act in a particular way.

It’s really crucial. I say this as somebody who’s worked on climate since the 80s, but it’s not the science that tells us what to do.

It’s also the science, along with values and interests and experience, that helps us shape and frame the science that really matters.

And why that matters is we basically block the politics out. And we block out that you can get different answers from the same data by asking the question differently or different questions.

And if we block that out, what we’re doing is being authoritarian, because we’re just giving one answer.

We’re hiding the values that give you that one answer, and then for those people who don’t share those values, by doing that, we’re being authoritarian. And instead of prompting compliance, we provoke a backlash, an authoritarian backlash.

So when science laments the post-truth authoritarianism that it experiences in many areas, it’s I think to a large extent seeing itself in the mirror.

And if it was more honest about its own uncertainties, its own politics, the way there’s always different answers you could get from any given model, we might get a more reasoned debate.

If you think back to the history of environmentalism and ask when was it most successful, you know everyone will have different views of this.

It’s in the spirit of my analysis that there’s different stories to be told.

But whether it’s whales, pesticides, chlorine chemicals, heavy metals. Although none of these issues have finally been won, there were some major victories took place in the history of environmentalism, rightly or wrongly, in which things were withdrawn from.

And across the board, the way that was done was against science, quite often expert scientists, academics, industry, government, universities, saying, "Look, we’ve done the science. It’s okay. We’ve done the calculations. We have models of the dispersion in the ocean."

And the environmentalists said, "We don’t believe your science. We think it’s been shaped by the kinds of power around it.

"And we’re talking about values. It’s just wrong to do this. And if you look at your model in a different way, you’ll get a different answer. You’ll get the answer we get."

And then again and again and again, environmentalists won on that kind of argument. By the time you roll around as as science and also especially environmentalism become institutionalized, you get exactly the arguments that lost being deployed in favour of climate change.

We’ve done the models. We’re global. We’ve modeled the entire global climate system. We thought up something called global mean temperature.

We are insisting it should be static, when in fact we know it’s dynamic, and we’re defining it to very high degrees of precision and saying our models will be the means by which the world addresses this problem.

So rather than doing it in terms of virtues and values and the kind of society we want to live in, which lost in the past.

We’re doing it on do what the science says, which lost in the past, arguably rightly, because you can’t do what the science says, and in the process we’re provoking exactly the backlash, as I mentioned earlier.

So that’s an example of the kinds of ways it’s been lost. That climate is of absolutely crucial importance, but it should be recognized to be a struggle, a democratic struggle, and not just based on science, because that’s the way you actually lose issues, not win them.

To behave like that is itself post-truth.

When science downplays its uncertainties, downplays the sensitivities, the way in which different assumptions in the model, which are equally reasonable, could get a different answer, the way in which values, emotions, virtues, ideologies all play a role in science, just like they do outside.

When it pretends that’s not the case, it is in fact behaving in a post-truth way, and so then it’s not surprising it gets a post-truth reaction.

So doubling down on that is exactly...it’s like throwing kerosene on the fire. It’s just not going to work to. Your self behaving in this authoritarian way and expect other authoritarianisms to go away.

We should be informing democracy and achieving these changes through democratic struggle. And science is absolutely essential to that, but only if it conducts itself in an honest way.

One thing that got me going with all this was in back in the ’90 s I was looking at risk assessments, cost-benefit analysis, life cycle assessments.

All these highly technical quantitative assessments in the energy sector.

Cutting a long story short, they were, the energy sector was the place where these things were developed to their most mature, sophisticated form. And if you looked at any given study, you got this really confident idea.

This is what the risks of nuclear are compared to renewables, compared to gas, or whatever it is.

The same with the other methods I mentioned.

And then every single time you stand back and you look at the literature as a whole, not just peer-reviewed literature, but the literature embodied in law.

So the most kind of authoritatively treated source of data on these things, and you found you could get any answer you like across that peer-reviewed literature.

It depends on the framing. The models give you an answer that depends on how you frame the question.

And that for me kind of radicalized me because I realized that none of the committees, none of the reports around the world were fully representing what the literature they were consulting told us, that you can get all kinds of different answers.

And what matters is not just the one answer, the risk, the cost, environmental costs, the ecosystem service.

What matters is how that changes depending on assumptions, that’s how science should speak to policy, but also to society, telling us how these things depend.

The reason I said that, a lot of people talk about lamenting the fact we have policy-based evidence rather than evidence-based policy, and it’s a good point.

You know, you get all kinds of practices making things up all the time, all over the place in every sector.

But my point wasn’t to lambast that. It wasn’t to say, to lament yet again "you guys are just stitching it up." It was to say "Actually, I’ve never yet seen an area where the evidence compels a single policy."

So even when you do get the best quality evidence, it is never without uncertainties. It’s never without differences of implication for action, depending on which discipline was actually most influential, how the questions were asked, what the baselines were, etc. etc.

So I have yet to see any body of analysis based on evidence that compels a single decision.

So when you hear people talking about evidence-based policy as if there were only one policy that could have been based on the evidence, they’re basically again being post-truth.

They’re (to be a bit more colourful about it, they’re telling porkies."

Because there will always be values, interests, assumptions at work, and it’s not a bad thing. It’s inevitable.

That’s how science, you know, depends. For instance, on BSE whether vets or were the epidemiologists in charge? He got a very different answer.

And in COVID, you know, again, we-I mean, it’s still too early to say, as Mao said, I think about the French Revolution, was it? But it’s too early to say.

But you can still see that what was the best way to act on the available evidence, economic as well as epidemiological, and the different ways of interpreting the epidemiological evidence.

It’s very clear now that it’s not so clear-cut what a particular country should do.

Different countries do different things. There are different ways of looking back on it, looking at the time and seeing what was good and what was bad.

So, without taking position on either side, it’s far from clear that there was a single definitive action that should have been taken.

I defy anyone to actually come back and defend that. There’ll be a matter of judgment as between really quite radically different policies.

So COVID is an example of this. I think we had to pretend there was one policy because it was so stressful.

Politicians had to pretend because otherwise they would have to hide behind their chief scientists, literally sometimes, literally behind them on the podium, hiding behind them because they needed that authority to protect them from the inevitable uncertainties that everyone believed were really there, even though they weren’t acknowledging it in the graphs.

I mean, blame management, trust, public acceptance.

These things are the most important commodities in politics. So yeah, and it’s you know apocryphally, people have all kinds of anecdotes out on these advisory committees.

I’ve served a little bit on some of them. You know, the number of times in which the politicians will intimate, "I won’t hesitate to hide behind you," almost as a joke.

But so you know, scientists respond to that in different ways. But by and large, they think, "Well, okay, we’ve got to be responsible. Let’s give these guys a single prescriptive answer, even though we know among ourselves that we could have got a different answer, but we’ve got a responsibility not to do an to do to do an elevator pitch."

You know, not to give on the one hand, on the other, as Margaret Thatcher said, "Save me from the two-handed economist. I want a one-handed economist."

She wants it because of justification, but actually, it’s a responsibility of the economist, or in this case, a scientist, to actually explain how it does depend. It always does depend.

If they don’t explain that, then they are failing, I would say science, and failing society, failing democracy.

Other things are really complicated. there’s a lot of real challenges. I don’t want to pretend it’s easier than it really is.

But actually, we shouldn’t be paralyzed by this. Look at science itself. When it developed in the 17th century, motto of the Royal Society, nullius in verba, that was basically saying that principles of accountability, of argument, of deliberation really mattered, of treating people more equally than many institutions do. That’s not the opposite of democracy. That is democracy.

Science was about, in many ways, democratizing knowledge.

You know, you needed to argue, you need to show evidence and do analyzes in rigorous ways. But it should be open to anyone to do that, and to any perspective, no matter how ridiculous it sounds, if it can substantiate itself.

So science and democracy are not on opposite sides.

So I think, rather than counterpointing them, like science is against democracy, we can’t trust democracy, going to undermine science, actually, see it the other way round: that science is an embodiment of democracy.

It’s when it is at its best. It’s when it’s being democratic about the ability to challenge power inside science, and that’s how we solve the problems of science.

It’s also how we solve the problems at the moment of democracy, which science is, sadly, because it’s forced to be more authoritarian in pretending a singular truth.

It’s forced into that not by democracy, but by power that is also eroding democracy.

Science, when it comes to advise policymakers, yes, please do your best, but don’t think of yourself just giving a single expedient answer so that a politician goes away happy and can act without worrying about blame.

Inform society at large about the assumptions that went into that.

Show how it depends, and if you do that, you’re informing democracy as much as the powerful actors who are, you know, maybe conferring the patronage on the scientists.

Science fails when it’s not being plural enough.

It needs to be plural about who’s involved, about the questions that are asked, about the disciplines that get around the table, about how it conveys its interpretations of its understandings out to society, and it needs to just not be scared of representing that plurality because with that comes the conditions.

It’s not just anything goes. It’s not plural for plurality’s sake.

It’s then saying under what conditions you get answer X or answer Y, and that’s more scientific.

It’s more rigorous to behave in that way.

When science does that, it’s being more scientific when it’s plural. So I think science fails most when it reduces all those kinds of plurality.

#935. Champions League power rankings: PSG remain a joke – but who is catching them?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Paris Saint-Germain and Real Madrid are the only teams to still have 100 per cent records after Liverpool’s defeat at Fenerbahce

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It was largely business as usual last month in the Champions League as Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona kept on scoring and Arsenal and Bayern Munich returned to winning ways while remaining unbeaten.

But the story of the round belonged to Como, who made history by beating Lens 9-1 away from home and equalling the record for the most goals scored in a single Champions League game. Cesc Fabregas’s impressive side now sit fourth in the league phase standings, behind PSG, Real Madrid and Arsenal.

Meanwhile, there was a frustrating defeat for Liverpool at Fenerbahce, but Manchester United produced a stunning comeback to beat Roma and potentially save Michael Carrick’s job, with Matheus Cunha scoring twice on a remarkable night at Old Trafford.

We compiled our 36-team power rankings by combining team’s previous performance in the Champions League, their results in the competition so far, and the likelihood of them going all the way this season.

Agree or disagree with our standings ahead of matchweek five? Let us know and have your say in the comments below.

The reigning champions are making a mockery of suggestions that they are slow starters in the Champions League. Luis Enrique’s back-to-back champions finished outside the top eight in both of their previous successes but have started this campaign on fire in Europe. PSG were 4-0 up after just 17 minutes at Villarreal, and that was without Ousmane Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. The French champions will be without the brilliant Georgian for the rest of the season after he suffered a ruptured ACL and has been joined on the sidelines by Desire Doue, who suffered the same injury during a 3-2 win over Nice on Saturday.

Defeats to Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League and Real Madrid in LaLiga ended their winning start under Hansi Flick and perhaps raised the same concerns over whether their defence holds up come the knockout stages. But Lamine Yamal is arguably the world’s best player on current form and Raphinha isn’t too bad, either. The Brazilian made it an astonishing 19 goals and three assists in just 13 matches across LaLiga and the Champions League with his double in the 3-0 win over Aston Villa at Camp Nou.

Mikel Arteta’s got the result they needed in Prague, even if a difficult second-half performance made it a bit of a struggle. An entertaining draw last time out at Bayern Munich, who have such a strong home record, gave a good account of whether the Premier League champions can take the next step against a heavyweight side in the business end of the Champions League. A frustrating stalemate with Dortmund brings them back into a scrap to secure that coveted top eight position, rather than a top-two seed and home advantage throughout the knockout stages.

Bayern returned to winning ways with a professional win against Atletico Madrid – and the big surprise was that Harry Kane was not on the scoresheet. The Ballon d’Or holder’s 10-match scoring run in the Champions League came to an end at the Metropolitano, missing the chance to equal Cristiano Ronaldo’s record, and Kane will now be out until the “business end” of the season due to an ankle injury.

Perhaps chaos is the new normal under Jose Mourinho. Real Madrid trailed late on in Athens but Kylian Mbappe equalised before Fede Valverde scored a stunning winner in stoppage time. Jude Bellingham also scored an outrageous flick. Somehow with maximum points, despite trailing Roma 3-1 at the Stadio Olimpico, and Inter and RB Leipzig spurning chances to take the lead at the Bernabeu, the 15-time Champions League winners continue to find a way. Romping to a 5-1 win over PSV, despite trailing, shows the firepower this team still has.

Three defeats from four in the Premier League have the shine off an impressive start for Enzo Maresca’s side, while uncertainty off the pitch remains as well. But a battling win at RB Leipzig, with a customary Erling Haaland goal, was a good response, even if City have now gone nine games without a clean sheet in all competitions. Another sloppy performance with the return of Kevin De Bruyne and Napoli, City now face a mouthwatering trip to Barcelona and likely require a result to avoid dropping out of the top eight.

Liverpool have conceded three goals in three consecutive games in the Champions League or European Cup for the first time and the manner of their “messy” collapse against Fenerbahce was a concern. The nature of Liverpool’s squad means Andoni Iraola has needed to rotate in Champions League but Liverpool’s performance in Istanbul underlined the task he faces. In-form Club Brugge can’t be taken lightly after the international break.

WOW. If Como announced themselves by thrashing Manchester United, the Champions League debutants stole the show this week with a NINE-goal dismantling of poor Lens. Cesc Fabregas’s stylish side became the first team to score nine goals away from home in the Champions League or European Cup since 1971. The Italian side are certainly making a name for themselves. Those games against PSG and Barcelona at the end of the league phase are going to be fascinating.

After starting with back-to-back defeats, how badly Inter needed to respond with back-to-back wins. A comfortable win at Feyenoord also came after the Milan derby defeat, with Pio Esposito stepping up amid Lautaro Martinez’s continued absence.

Defeat in Istanbul followed defeat at the Camp Nou puts Unai Emery’s new-look Aston Villa in a tricky spot: outside of the top eight and heading towards the playoff round. Bright showings from the refreshed attacking line-up of Nicolas Jackson, Johan Manzambi, Ibrahim Mbaye and Alysson have helped the Europa League winners retaining their identity under Emery despite the huge squad turnover in the summer, but the closing three fixtures will be tough, and they may have to settle for an additional tie in the knockout stage.

#934. Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows

Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the trend.

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

#933. Underperforming Manchester City are an accident waiting to happen

Enzo Maresca had two home games in four days to get Manchester City into decent shape for Sunday’s clash against Arsenal, which now feels like a must-win. On Tuesday, however, they ended up being taunted by Rasmus Hojlund on another evening that raised more questions than answers.

It is now one win in seven for Maresca, who cannot keep a clean sheet and has a £327m midfield that have played well individually, but is yet to form a unit. Worryingly, their reliable source of goals, Erling Haaland, had his quietest game of the season. It required Rayan Cherki to rescue a point against Napoli.

Maresca needs to find a solution in the next five days before heading to the Emirates to face the champions in what could be a defining weekend for the season. Defeat would put them nine points off the pace, with Maresca still trying to find his best combination of players to pick.

Club captain Rúben Dias was on the bench here and Josko Gvardiol was left out of the draw against Fulham at the weekend, which also ended as a draw rather than a morale-boosting win to get City out of their slump.

There is enough quality in City’s midfield to trouble Arsenal, but the conundrum for Maresca is how to fit them all into his system. Elliot Anderson was pushed towards the right against Napoli rather than in a central position to control the game, while Ayyoub Bouaddi was often alongside “inverted” full-back Nico O’Reilly.

Bouaddi showed his attacking instincts with City’s first equaliser; incredibly his first goal as a professional. There cannot be many £86m players who have yet to score in senior football. Enzo Fernandez also started against Napoli but was quiet before being taken off for the last half an hour.

Kevin De Bruyne has been lined up for a January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch club working on a deal to land one of the Premier League’s greatest players when the window opens.

De Bruyne, 35, has been at Napoli since the start of last season but it is understood that a move away from the Serie A club is now on the horizon. He is still under contract at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona so PSV will pay a fee to land him as they look to retain their Eredivisie title.

At Manchester City, De Bruyne won six Premier League titles and was part of their Treble-winning team that won the Champions League. During the last 18 months at Napoli he has suffered injury issues, had a row with team-mate on the pitch and was quoted as saying he was glad Antonio Conte left as head coach.

“Not a lot I can say for the moment,” said De Bruyne when asked about his future. “I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

“There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.”

It is matchday five of the Champions League as Manchester City host Napoli at the Etihad. These sides last met back in September 2025, with Manchester City winning 2-0 at home courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku. Manchester City’s cause was helped by an early red card for Napoli’s Giovanni Di Lorenzo. Napoli’s only win over Manchester City came all the way back in November 2011 when they won 2-1 after a double from Edinson Cavani.

Manchester City have won three of their opening four Champions League matches this season, with their only defeat coming at home against back-to-back champions PSG. They drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday, which means they are now without a league win in four games.

“We are always looking to win games, no matter the competition,” Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca said. “For sure, the four games in a row in the Premier League that we did not win has been a shame. Tomorrow [tonight] we have a chance to win the game and continue our path in the Champions League that at the moment has been very good. First of all, it is important to qualify and then probably, if you are not able to finish in the top eight, you have two more games that with the amount of games that we have, it is always important to reduce games. So the target is to try and finish in the top eight.”

Napoli, managed by Massimiliano Allegri, have struggled thus far in this season’s Champions League, winning just one of their opening four games and are all the way down in 27th. They come into tonight’s match off the back of a 1-0 home win over Torino in Serie A on the weekend courtesy of former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay’s winning goal. However, they still sit down in eighth in the Italian top flight, a massive 14 points off the top through just 12 games.

“This match will not be decisive,” Allegri said. “It is a simple mathematical equation, but obviously we will try to do well, even against a great team like Manchester City. It will be a beautiful and fascinating challenge and we want to play to the best of our ability. Ultimately, our goal is to qualify. We must not repeat the mistakes we made in Porto, where we played a great game for 70 minutes and then let ourselves go, conceding chances too easily. We will have to be able to play both with and without possession.”

Team news from the Etihad to follow shortly.

#931. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

#930. Rasmus Hojlund reveals intense Bruno Fernandes reaction to Michael Carrick sacking

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Hojlund, who scored for Napoli in Manchester against City on Tuesday, is still in touch with former Man United teammate Fernandes and the pair discussed the fallout from Carrick’s dismissal

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bruno Fernandes was devastated Michael Carrick was sacked as Manchester United manager, according to his former teammate Rasmus Hojlund.

The Napoli striker, who completed his £44m move away from Old Trafford in the summer, is convinced that his old team, who are 19th in the Premier League, will only have a temporary stay in the relegation zone.

And Hojlund, a boyhood United fan who joined them for £64m in 2023, believes they have too much quality to go down.

The Denmark international was back in Manchester to score for Napoli against City in Tuesday’s 2-2 draw in the Champions League.

And he said: “I am watching all the games I can, especially from the red side of Manchester. It is unfortunate [that United are struggling].”

United have not won in their last nine league games, dating back to August, and lost 4-0 to Liverpool on Sunday in Mauricio Pochettino’s first match in charge.

They are second from bottom but Hojlund is not worried. “It is a temporary picture, I think they will get back to the top, the Premier League is like this,” he said. “I read the other day that Bournemouth were in the relegation zone after a couple of games, now they have won the last five games and are in the top half of the table.

“They have got a lot of quality, I have seen the guys training day by day and I know the players really well and they have got a great squad, good leaders, good professionals so I am sure they will turn it around. Hopefully they will get it right with Mauricio.”

Captain Fernandes was dropped by Carrick after questioning his tactics in the Champions League defeat to Como but he and Diogo Dalot caught up with Hojlund when Denmark faced Portugal and the forward said they were upset the manager was losing his job.

“In the international break when I spoke with Bruno and Diogo, they were all obviously devastated that Michael was going but also looking forward to some change,” Hojlund added. “I am still speaking with Patrick [Dorgu, his Denmark teammate] and I just wish the guys all the best and I am sure they will turn it around this season.”

Hojlund, who scored 26 goals in 95 games in two seasons at Old Trafford, said playing for United comes with great pressure, making it harder in the bad times.

“United is a massive club and you can’t take anything away from that,” he said. “There are so many people following the club around the world and you can’t really escape from it, it is almost too high when it is good and almost too low when it is bad so it is all about trying to be in that middle and now I think I tried both the highs and the lows there. The pressure is part of the club. It comes with playing for Man United.”

For a generation of football fans in the UK, Soccer AM was a staple of their Saturday morning routine.

The Sky TV show combined football, comedy and celebrity guests, all with a healthy dose of general chaos.

When TV newcomer and longtime Soccer AM fan Max Rushden landed the co-presenter job alongside Helen Chamberlain in 2008, he was thrown into a world he had never experienced before.

“Getting the job was mad because I'd never done a TV show in my life, and it definitely showed in the first two years,” Rushden tells FourFourTwo.

“But I loved the show – I was a fan of the week in 2000 and watched it religiously until about two or three years before getting the job, so the whole thing was surreal.”

Rushden’s journey from avid viewer to presenter had plenty of twists, including an audition for another iconic British TV programme.

“I was doing a breakfast show on Radio London, but I had to go back to reading the news because I wasn't famous,” he continues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I thought, ‘OK, I'll make a show and send it to everybody' – the only two people who replied were from the Travel Channel, who said I was boring, and Sky Sports, who asked me to go in for a chat.

“I bowled in, chatted about Cambridge and Soccer AM for an hour. They said they might have something for me in a couple of months, but I didn't expect much.”

After leaving the audition with low expectations, Rushden continued to explore other possibilities.

“In the meantime, I'd got an audition for Blue Peter,” he reveals before receiving a life-changing telephone call.

“Before I went to it, I got a call from Sky and they asked, “Do you want to do Soccer AM?” My head just exploded and I was trying to play it cool.

"I signed the contract and s**t myself for a month before the show started.”

#928. Wirtz follows Keegan and Dalglish with defining performance as Liverpool No 7

It had to be this way. Liverpool No 7s have historically defined matches against Club Brugge, so it was entirely appropriate that Florian Wirtz preserved that rich heritage.

The late Kevin Keegan thrashed home a free-kick at this stadium 50 years ago to win Liverpool the Uefa Cup and Sir Kenny Dalglish was the hero at Wembley in 1978 when his deft finish ensured the European Cup was retained.

That jersey means those who have subsequently worn it have had high standards to keep. Although this fixture did not carry the heft of past glorious occasions, it was symbolic that Wirtz, the current incumbent, decorated this contest and propelled Liverpool a step closer to the knockout phase.

On another night Alexander Isak would have expected his two goals to take the headlines, but he would have appreciated more than anyone the magic spells that Wirtz kept casting. The Swede had a glorious view of the strike that essentially secured three points in Belgium’s frozen north.

The idea of Brugge playing in the biggest club fixture of all, sadly, seems fanciful now given how much the landscape has changed. But they are a progressive side, full of attacking wit, and they had ambitions and, on another evening, would have done some damage.

How often, though, do you see sides these days undo their good work by being overambitious when playing out from the back? Yann Sommer has had a distinguished career, the Swiss goalkeeper has played for Bayern Munich and Inter Milan, but he is 37 and his aberration was decisive.

He put Kyriani Sabbe in all manner of trouble with a loose pass, Bradley Barcola picked the right-back’s pocket and nudged it on swiftly to Dominik Szoboszlai, who in turn fed Isak. With the goal at his mercy from six yards, the striker was never going to miss.
